item.title: Robots to assemble solar panels in two minutes for 457 MW US project
item.description:
Robots to assemble solar panels in two minutes for a 457 megawatt US project. This one comes from Interesting Engineering, written by Muskan Bhatia and published November thirteenth, 2026.

Here is the headline idea. A large solar farm being built in Navarro County, Texas, is turning to robots to put its panels together. The project is called Tormes Solar, and when it's finished it will have a capacity of 457 megawatts. The developer is Matrix Renewables, a Spanish company, and the robotic system comes from a US company called Terabase Energy. Their platform is called Terafab V2.

So what exactly is Terafab V2? The easiest way to picture it is as a small, portable factory that gets set up right on the construction site. Terabase describes it as a modular factory. Instead of crews assembling solar hardware piece by piece out in the field, the parts are brought to this on-site production line, where robots do much of the assembly. And interestingly, the system isn't just hardware. It also helps manage and plan the whole construction project, which we'll come back to in a minute.

The upgraded version, V2, launched this past April. According to Terabase, once it's up and running continuously, it can assemble one unit in about two minutes. At that pace, the company says, it can turn out about twenty megawatts of solar capacity in a single week. The system has been field tested, and right now it's optimized for one specific combination of equipment: First Solar's Series 7 modules, and trackers made by Nextpower.

Let's talk about why anyone would want to do this. Building a utility-scale solar farm is a lot of repetitive, physical labor. It's time consuming, it's expensive, and moving bulky materials around a huge site adds even more cost. Terabase's answer is to bring the production line to the farm and automate it.

Here's how the process works, step by step. First, the raw materials get delivered to the site. That means the solar panels themselves, plus the metal hardware: frames, brackets, mounts, and long steel pieces called tracker torque tubes. Those torque tubes are the backbone of a solar tracker. They're long rotating steel tubes that let the panels tilt and follow the sun across the sky during the day.

Next, the robots go to work. They fasten the photovoltaic modules onto those torque tubes, building up finished assemblies. Then comes quality control. The system uses AI-assisted tools to check that everything has been placed and attached correctly.

After that, autonomous vehicles, which the company calls rovers, pick up the finished assemblies and carry them out across the solar farm to where they'll be installed. And finally, there's still a human step at the end. Workers in the field take the assembled units off the rovers and set them onto tracker supports that have already been fixed into the ground.

One of the selling points is how mobile all of this is. Terabase says one of these modular robotic systems can be set up in roughly four hours. That means it can be deployed quickly, and it can also be picked up and moved to a new spot on the site as construction progresses across what can be a very large piece of land. And you're not limited to one. A single project can run multiple assembly line modules at the same time to increase overall output.

Now, back to that software side. Terabase emphasizes that it isn't just dropping robots onto a field. The platform combines the automation hardware with software for planning, tracking materials, and handling logistics. It also includes a digital replica of the construction site, sometimes called a digital twin. That gives project managers a live view of what's happening, so they can monitor progress and coordinate the work more effectively.

What kind of improvement are we talking about? Terabase claims that compared with conventional methods for installing utility-scale solar, its automated approach can double labor productivity. But the company adds an important caveat: actual results depend on how the project is configured, how fully the equipment is used, and the conditions at the particular site. So, doubling is the company's own claim, and real-world mileage will vary.

There's also some track record here. The first-generation Terafab platform has been available since 2022. Terabase says it's been used to install about 40 megawatts of tracker-mounted solar capacity across several US projects, including sites in Arizona and Texas. Worth putting that in perspective: 40 megawatts total from the first generation, versus a 457 megawatt project now, and a claimed pace of 20 megawatts a week for the new version. This Texas deployment is a significant step up in scale.

Looking ahead, Terabase has two main goals. One is to make the system work with more kinds of solar modules and trackers, beyond the First Solar and Nextpower combination it's tuned for today. The other is to automate that last manual step. Remember, workers still have to lift the assembled units onto the tracker supports in the ground. The company is developing additional robots to handle that final installation step too.

So, to sum it up. A 457 megawatt solar farm in Texas is using Terabase Energy's Terafab V2, a portable robotic factory that assembles solar units on site in about two minutes each, checks them with AI-assisted tools, and sends them out on autonomous rovers for installation. It sets up in about four hours, can be moved around the site, and pairs the robots with planning software and a digital model of the project. The company claims it can produce twenty megawatts a week and double labor productivity, though it notes results depend on the site. Humans still handle the final placement for now, but Terabase is working on robots for that as well. That's the story from Interesting Engineering.

Source: https://interestingengineering.com/energy/texas-solar-farm-deploys-robots

item.title: NuScale Power Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for NuScale Power, ticker S-M-R. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. NuScale released the numbers on Thursday, November fifth, twenty twenty-six, after the close, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were Jennifer Hills, vice president of finance; John Hopkins, president and chief executive officer; and Ramsey Hamady, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the company's official earnings-call transcript, its press release furnished with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and contemporaneous coverage of the results, including published consensus estimates. I will cover the results against expectations, what management did and did not guide, the company's key points, notable analyst questions from the official transcript, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. This was not a revenue quarter, and it was not meant to look like one. NuScale reported revenue of two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars for the third quarter, which the company rounded to three-tenths of a million dollars on the call. That compares with eight point two million dollars in the same quarter a year earlier, a decline of about ninety-seven percent. The drop was expected in kind, if not necessarily in size. The year-ago quarter included Front-End Engineering and Design Phase Two work for the RoPower project in Romania, work that was completed in late twenty twenty-five, with no comparable activity this year. Published consensus estimates still looked for more. MarketBeat and TipRanks both put the revenue estimate at three point six six million dollars, so the result missed by about three point four million dollars.

On the bottom line, the company did better than the main published estimates. The loss per share was eleven cents, compared with a loss of one dollar and eighty-five cents a year earlier. MarketBeat and TipRanks put the consensus at a loss of twelve cents, a one-cent beat. Net loss was forty-five point seven million dollars, narrowing from a net loss of five hundred thirty-two point six million dollars in the third quarter of twenty twenty-five. That year-ago comparison is distorted by a huge drop in general and administrative expense, which fell to twenty-seven point nine million dollars from five hundred nineteen point two million dollars. The company did not present this quarter as a sudden burst of operating earnings. It presented it as a step from design work into physical manufacturing, funded by a very large cash pile, while commercial orders are still pending.

The company did not give formal financial guidance. That is an official fact, not an omission I am filling in. Hamady said on the call that NuScale does not provide guidance as a general matter, and that it wants to be able to give the Street guidance on margins and profitability once an original equipment manufacturer agreement is in place. What management did say is that operating expenses should remain fairly constant for now, that capital deployment will continue at a measured and disciplined pace as the company funds first-article fabrication with Doosan Enerbility and advances engineering and licensing readiness ahead of an ENTRA1 original equipment manufacturer agreement, and that it is not communicating any other significant investments publicly at this time.

Let me walk through the financials with that context.

Revenue of two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars produced a gross margin of one hundred thirty-three thousand dollars, compared with two point seven million dollars of gross margin a year earlier. Cost of sales was one hundred forty-eight thousand dollars, down from five point five million dollars. For the first nine months, revenue was nine hundred twenty-one thousand dollars, compared with twenty-nine point seven million dollars a year earlier. With nine-month revenue still under a million dollars, any full-year estimate that assumed a sudden jump in the fourth quarter would have required a very large fourth-quarter number. One later commentary noted that a lingering full-year estimate would have implied about nineteen point five million dollars of fourth-quarter revenue. The company did not guide to that, and I am not going to treat it as management's number.

Operating expenses were sixty-five million dollars, compared with five hundred forty-nine million dollars a year earlier. Research and development was eighteen point zero million dollars, up seven point zero million dollars year over year, mainly because of higher costs to advance the design maturity of NuScale Power Module components. General and administrative expense, as I mentioned, collapsed from the year-ago figure, which had been swollen by items that did not repeat at anything like the same scale. Other expenses rose by eight point one million dollars year over year, the company said, in part because engineers and project personnel were working on fewer commercial projects, so less cost was allocated into cost of sales, and in part because of higher compensation as the company ramped resources for supply-chain readiness. Investment income was nineteen point one million dollars, up from five point eight million dollars, reflecting a stronger cash position and higher yields. That interest income is a meaningful offset to the operating burn, but it is not module revenue.

Liquidity is the financial story investors can actually underwrite today. NuScale ended the quarter with approximately one point nine billion dollars in cash, cash equivalents, and short- and long-term investments, compared with about nine hundred sixteen million dollars a year earlier. One commentary separately noted that cash and equivalents, the portion not placed in investments, came to five hundred thirteen million dollars at September thirtieth. Long-lead material work in process was sixty-nine point seven million dollars, reflecting the continued accumulation of inventory and materials for module fabrication. Hamady said the company has adequate liquidity to fund first-article fabrication with Doosan and to advance engineering and licensing readiness ahead of an ENTRA1 original equipment manufacturer agreement, and that it expects capital deployment to remain measured and disciplined.

Hopkins used the quarter to argue that NuScale has moved from development to physical production. The centerpiece is a contract with Doosan Enerbility for first-article production of the upper reactor coolant system of the NuScale Power Module. Hopkins said the contract moves the company's Nuclear Regulatory Commission-approved design into actual build and sets the foundation for all modules to follow. In the press release he said, quote, This was a significant quarter for NuScale as we progressed from development to physical production of our first commercial NuScale Power Module, end quote. On the call he added that customers and investors need evidence that modules can actually be built to nuclear quality standards and on schedule, and that first articles help provide that evidence and surface early issues before series production.

Around that milestone, management pointed to a supply chain of more than sixty specialized suppliers covering critical scopes such as fuel, major forgings, and module handling cranes. It said it completed first-of-a-kind fabrication for the passive emergency core cooling system with MillenniTEK. It added one new E-two center in the quarter, bringing the global total to thirteen, to support operator training and technology awareness. It also said it has deployed nuclear-specific artificial intelligence tools across engineering and knowledge management to accelerate design workflows.

The product itself has not changed in the headline specifications. Each NuScale Power Module is designed for seventy-seven megawatts of electricity, using standard light-water reactor technology and conventional nuclear fuel available today. The design is certified for plants with up to twelve modules, or nine hundred twenty-four megawatts in total. Management estimated that fifty to sixty percent of prior licensing work is reusable for future domestic construction and operation license applications, often called COLA work. Hopkins also emphasized that NuScale holds what it called the only Nuclear Regulatory Commission-approved small modular reactor design in the world, and that the technology uses proven passive safety features and can be deployed where customers need reliable power.

Hopkins's prepared remarks spent most of their time on readiness rather than on the quarter's tiny revenue line, and that is the case he wants shareholders to hear. He said recent quarters had been about commercial readiness as a technology provider and original equipment manufacturer, and that this quarter took a significant step: the company progressed from development to physical production. Quote, We are no longer simply designing and planning, we are manufacturing, end quote. He described the Doosan agreement as a landmark, and said that while ENTRA1 continues work to finalize arrangements required for project development, NuScale is not standing still. It is strengthening original equipment manufacturer capabilities, deepening supply-chain readiness, and positioning for full-scale production.

His capital message was conservative. The approach, he said, is to stay disciplined on capital, hit the milestones the company can control, and ensure that when commercial agreements are finalized, NuScale can deliver without unnecessary delay or added risk. He said the company is ready with approved technology, proven fuel technology, an engineering and regulatory foundation, strategic partnerships, and a global supply chain. He tied that readiness to a broader demand story: artificial intelligence, data-center growth, industrial energy needs, and energy security, all of which, in his telling, are creating demand for reliable, affordable, carbon-free baseload power.

He also walked through the work that is already underway while ENTRA1 advances customer engagements. NuScale, he said, is advancing detailed engineering, locking in key suppliers, and preparing to support the construction and operating license application process, including for a potential Tennessee Valley Authority project. The licensing team, he said, is already preparing to support that application. He called it familiar ground, because the company holds a Nuclear Regulatory Commission design certification and standard design approvals, and because it completed substantial licensing work on the earlier carbon-free power project. A meaningful portion of that prior effort, he said, is directly reusable for T.V.A. or any other future domestic project, which should compress both schedule and cost relative to a first-time application.

Engineering teams, he added, are drawing on experience from RoPower and other programs. Once an engineering, procurement, and construction contractor is selected, NuScale would support that work under a separate contract covering its proprietary design, keeping the company involved in design integrity while the contractor leads overall project delivery. Further along the timeline, NuScale is also positioning to support operator training, start-up consulting, and fuel-preparation activities in coordination with Framatome. Hopkins was careful to say those are longer-dated opportunities, but that the company is laying the groundwork now, and that many of these steps run in parallel rather than in a single-file sequence.

He also named specific supply-chain moves meant to take long-lead risk off the critical path. Framatome, he said, is completing NuScale fuel design well ahead of customer commitments under a dedicated agreement. Paragon has been awarded a contract to finish production development of safety instrumentation and control systems, with NuScale jointly owning the underlying intellectual property. Across the broader supply base, the company is driving dual or tertiary sourcing on the majority of packages so that no single supplier becomes a constraint. For shareholders, he said, the Doosan investment positions NuScale to execute when orders are secured, with component costs expected to be recovered through the owner's contractual payment schedule under a future original equipment manufacturer agreement.

Hopkins was equally clear that T.V.A. is the immediate priority, but not the only conversation. He said NuScale continues to engage utilities, hyperscalers, and major industrial customers, and that the business model combines ENTRA1's commercial development capabilities with NuScale's approved technology, supply chain, and manufacturing readiness. For shareholders, he said, the opportunity is not simply one project. It is the potential to establish a scalable global original equipment manufacturer business capable of supporting multiple customers and deployments over decades. He also said the company expects to provide further updates as discussions mature into actionable commercial commitments. That last clause is worth holding onto, because the call itself did not convert those discussions into named, dated orders.

The commercial pipeline, though, is still mostly about agreements that have not been signed. The press release said NuScale continues to support its commercial partner, ENTRA1 Energy, in dialogue with the Tennessee Valley Authority on what the company described as the development of the largest commercial nuclear power deployment program in United States history. That is the company's characterization of the opportunity, not a signed, funded order. On the call, Hopkins said the process continues, that the company is optimistic, and that what NuScale can control is building the capacity to execute. He called the move into first article a major milestone in preparation for a project such as T.V.A., because it takes the design into physical hardware and helps derisk the path from engineering to commercial delivery. He also acknowledged that the process has been lengthy.

Hamady later clarified the sequencing, which matters a great deal. A power purchase agreement between ENTRA1 and T.V.A. is not itself the sale of modules. After such a power purchase agreement, the company would expect work on pre-engineering, predelivery services, licensing applications, and other engineering services. The sale of the module would come with an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1. Until those agreements exist, the one point nine billion dollar cash pile and the Doosan first-article work are the tangible evidence, and the T.V.A. opportunity remains a process.

Romania is the other named project, and it is quieter, not clearer. The year-ago revenue was tied to RoPower front-end work that has ended. Asked for an update, Hopkins said there is a new administration in place, that there have been some public announcements, and that NuScale continues dialogue with both RoPower and Nuclearelectrica, one of the major shareholders. He said he had recently sent a request to visit with the current administration to get insight into where the government is headed. Quote, So at this time, that's all we know, end quote.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the official transcript.

George Gianarikas of Canaccord Genuity asked for a timeline on a potential commercial agreement with T.V.A. and on other commercial activity, noting that the procurement of long-lead items would seem to indicate some confidence. Hopkins declined to give a date. He said the process continues, that the company is optimistic, and that first-article production is what NuScale can control while it waits. Gianarikas then asked Hamady how much operating-expense growth investors should expect. Hamady said the company does not provide guidance, discussed keeping operating expenses fairly constant, and later in the call the company and coverage noted that operating expenses had been maintained within a plus or minus five percent band for eight straight quarters. Management also said expenses would be expected to grow once NuScale is engaged with a project, with increased spending spread between operating expenses and cost of goods sold.

Nate Pendleton of Texas Capital Bank and Eric Stine of Craig-Hallum asked about commercial and licensing next steps, including what happens once a project is far enough along to support a construction and operating license application. The answers tracked Hopkins's prepared remarks: NuScale would look at revenues from engineering and related services, and a substantial share of prior licensing work, fifty to sixty percent by management's estimate, could be reused. That reusable work is one of the few quantitative claims on the call about how a first commercial project might be cheaper or faster than a clean-sheet application. It is still an estimate, not a signed schedule.

Christopher Souther of Truist Securities asked Hamady to unpack the operating-expense comparison and the role of strategic investors from Korea and Japan. Hamady noted that some of the work with RoPower had wound down, as reflected in revenue, and used the question to talk about the company's Korean and Japanese strategic relationships as part of the manufacturing and commercialization push, including the Doosan work.

Craig Shere of Tuohy Brothers pressed on when the company could give the Street more formal financial guidance. Hamady said NuScale will be able to give guidance soon, and that the objective is to help the Street understand profitability once an original equipment manufacturer agreement is in place. That is the cleanest guidance-about-guidance comment on the call. It also means today's sixty-five million dollars of quarterly operating expenses should not be lightly turned into a forward earnings model for a company that still has almost no product revenue.

Derek Soderberg of Cantor Fitzgerald asked about the path from a power purchase agreement to actual module production. That is the question that produced Hamady's sequencing clarification: a T.V.A. power purchase agreement would be between ENTRA1 and T.V.A., after which NuScale would expect pre-engineering and licensing work, with module sales arriving only with an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1.

Seth Basham of Wedbush Securities asked first about RoPower, which produced Hopkins's answer about the new Romanian administration, and then about other significant investments needed to move toward full-scale production besides the Doosan work, and the timing of those investments. Hamady's answer was short and clear. Quote, We do not have any other significant investments that we are communicating publicly at this time, end quote.

Hopkins closed by saying that while others remain in early stages of regulatory review, technology development, and fuel qualification, NuScale is advancing toward commercial deployment now. He said the focus is securing customer commitments, achieving manufacturing milestones, converting backlog into revenue, and building a scalable, profitable business. The next chapter, he said, will not be measured simply by milestones achieved, but by revenues generated, projects delivered, and lasting value to shareholders.

On the stock, the immediate read was not a simple punishment for the revenue miss. A TIKR report said NuScale rebounded fourteen percent the following morning after the narrower-than-expected loss, and argued that investors were not trading the stock on quarterly sales. That is one published account of the next-session move, not a closing print I am going to treat as the last word, and later commentary also pointed to lingering uncertainty around the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. process. The fair takeaway is that the market was looking through the near-zero revenue line to the cash position and to whether a commercial agreement is getting closer.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. process, and specifically the two agreements that would actually change the financial model: a power purchase agreement between ENTRA1 and T.V.A., and then an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1. Until those exist, first-article work is preparation, not a substitute for orders.

Second, whether management begins to give formal margin and profitability guidance after an original equipment manufacturer agreement, as Hamady said it wants to do.

Third, operating expenses and cash use. Sixty-five million dollars of quarterly operating expenses against one point nine billion dollars of liquidity is a long runway if expenses stay roughly flat, and a shorter one if a project start causes spending to step up. Investment income of nineteen point one million dollars this quarter is a cushion, not a business model.

Fourth, conversion of manufacturing milestones into recognized revenue. The Doosan first-article contract, the long-lead inventory of sixty-nine point seven million dollars, and the emergency-core-cooling fabrication work are evidence of a supply chain being stood up. They are not yet evidence of a revenue ramp.

Fifth, RoPower and the new Romanian administration. The last meaningful engineering revenue came from that project, and Hopkins's update was that the company is still waiting for clarity.

Sixth, the difference between a certified design and a sold plant. A seventy-seven megawatt module and a nine hundred twenty-four megawatt twelve-module plant are licensed concepts. The investment case now turns on whether a customer signs, funds, and schedules one.

Let me close with a short recap.

NuScale missed published revenue estimates with only two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars of third-quarter sales, down from eight point two million dollars a year earlier after RoPower front-end work ended, but it beat the main consensus on the loss per share, at eleven cents versus a twelve-cent estimated loss. The company held about one point nine billion dollars of liquidity, kept quarterly operating expenses at sixty-five million dollars, and did not issue formal financial guidance. Management's message was that NuScale has entered physical production through a Doosan first-article contract, while the larger commercial prizes, especially the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. opportunity, remain in process. The official transcript makes the sequencing explicit: a power purchase agreement would not itself be a module sale. The thing to watch is whether those agreements arrive, and whether the first-article work stays on schedule until they do.

Thanks for listening.

Author: NuScale Power
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this earnings brief for NuScale Power, ticker S-M-R. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. NuScale released the numbers on Thursday, November fifth, twenty twenty-six, after the close, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were Jennifer Hills, vice president of finance; John Hopkins, president and chief executive officer; and Ramsey Hamady, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the company's official earnings-call transcript, its press release furnished with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and contemporaneous coverage of the results, including published consensus estimates. I will cover the results against expectations, what management did and did not guide, the company's key points, notable analyst questions from the official transcript, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. This was not a revenue quarter, and it was not meant to look like one. NuScale reported revenue of two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars for the third quarter, which the company rounded to three-tenths of a million dollars on the call. That compares with eight point two million dollars in the same quarter a year earlier, a decline of about ninety-seven percent. The drop was expected in kind, if not necessarily in size. The year-ago quarter included Front-End Engineering and Design Phase Two work for the RoPower project in Romania, work that was completed in late twenty twenty-five, with no comparable activity this year. Published consensus estimates still looked for more. MarketBeat and TipRanks both put the revenue estimate at three point six six million dollars, so the result missed by about three point four million dollars.

On the bottom line, the company did better than the main published estimates. The loss per share was eleven cents, compared with a loss of one dollar and eighty-five cents a year earlier. MarketBeat and TipRanks put the consensus at a loss of twelve cents, a one-cent beat. Net loss was forty-five point seven million dollars, narrowing from a net loss of five hundred thirty-two point six million dollars in the third quarter of twenty twenty-five. That year-ago comparison is distorted by a huge drop in general and administrative expense, which fell to twenty-seven point nine million dollars from five hundred nineteen point two million dollars. The company did not present this quarter as a sudden burst of operating earnings. It presented it as a step from design work into physical manufacturing, funded by a very large cash pile, while commercial orders are still pending.

The company did not give formal financial guidance. That is an official fact, not an omission I am filling in. Hamady said on the call that NuScale does not provide guidance as a general matter, and that it wants to be able to give the Street guidance on margins and profitability once an original equipment manufacturer agreement is in place. What management did say is that operating expenses should remain fairly constant for now, that capital deployment will continue at a measured and disciplined pace as the company funds first-article fabrication with Doosan Enerbility and advances engineering and licensing readiness ahead of an ENTRA1 original equipment manufacturer agreement, and that it is not communicating any other significant investments publicly at this time.

Let me walk through the financials with that context.

Revenue of two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars produced a gross margin of one hundred thirty-three thousand dollars, compared with two point seven million dollars of gross margin a year earlier. Cost of sales was one hundred forty-eight thousand dollars, down from five point five million dollars. For the first nine months, revenue was nine hundred twenty-one thousand dollars, compared with twenty-nine point seven million dollars a year earlier. With nine-month revenue still under a million dollars, any full-year estimate that assumed a sudden jump in the fourth quarter would have required a very large fourth-quarter number. One later commentary noted that a lingering full-year estimate would have implied about nineteen point five million dollars of fourth-quarter revenue. The company did not guide to that, and I am not going to treat it as management's number.

Operating expenses were sixty-five million dollars, compared with five hundred forty-nine million dollars a year earlier. Research and development was eighteen point zero million dollars, up seven point zero million dollars year over year, mainly because of higher costs to advance the design maturity of NuScale Power Module components. General and administrative expense, as I mentioned, collapsed from the year-ago figure, which had been swollen by items that did not repeat at anything like the same scale. Other expenses rose by eight point one million dollars year over year, the company said, in part because engineers and project personnel were working on fewer commercial projects, so less cost was allocated into cost of sales, and in part because of higher compensation as the company ramped resources for supply-chain readiness. Investment income was nineteen point one million dollars, up from five point eight million dollars, reflecting a stronger cash position and higher yields. That interest income is a meaningful offset to the operating burn, but it is not module revenue.

Liquidity is the financial story investors can actually underwrite today. NuScale ended the quarter with approximately one point nine billion dollars in cash, cash equivalents, and short- and long-term investments, compared with about nine hundred sixteen million dollars a year earlier. One commentary separately noted that cash and equivalents, the portion not placed in investments, came to five hundred thirteen million dollars at September thirtieth. Long-lead material work in process was sixty-nine point seven million dollars, reflecting the continued accumulation of inventory and materials for module fabrication. Hamady said the company has adequate liquidity to fund first-article fabrication with Doosan and to advance engineering and licensing readiness ahead of an ENTRA1 original equipment manufacturer agreement, and that it expects capital deployment to remain measured and disciplined.

Hopkins used the quarter to argue that NuScale has moved from development to physical production. The centerpiece is a contract with Doosan Enerbility for first-article production of the upper reactor coolant system of the NuScale Power Module. Hopkins said the contract moves the company's Nuclear Regulatory Commission-approved design into actual build and sets the foundation for all modules to follow. In the press release he said, quote, This was a significant quarter for NuScale as we progressed from development to physical production of our first commercial NuScale Power Module, end quote. On the call he added that customers and investors need evidence that modules can actually be built to nuclear quality standards and on schedule, and that first articles help provide that evidence and surface early issues before series production.

Around that milestone, management pointed to a supply chain of more than sixty specialized suppliers covering critical scopes such as fuel, major forgings, and module handling cranes. It said it completed first-of-a-kind fabrication for the passive emergency core cooling system with MillenniTEK. It added one new E-two center in the quarter, bringing the global total to thirteen, to support operator training and technology awareness. It also said it has deployed nuclear-specific artificial intelligence tools across engineering and knowledge management to accelerate design workflows.

The product itself has not changed in the headline specifications. Each NuScale Power Module is designed for seventy-seven megawatts of electricity, using standard light-water reactor technology and conventional nuclear fuel available today. The design is certified for plants with up to twelve modules, or nine hundred twenty-four megawatts in total. Management estimated that fifty to sixty percent of prior licensing work is reusable for future domestic construction and operation license applications, often called COLA work. Hopkins also emphasized that NuScale holds what it called the only Nuclear Regulatory Commission-approved small modular reactor design in the world, and that the technology uses proven passive safety features and can be deployed where customers need reliable power.

Hopkins's prepared remarks spent most of their time on readiness rather than on the quarter's tiny revenue line, and that is the case he wants shareholders to hear. He said recent quarters had been about commercial readiness as a technology provider and original equipment manufacturer, and that this quarter took a significant step: the company progressed from development to physical production. Quote, We are no longer simply designing and planning, we are manufacturing, end quote. He described the Doosan agreement as a landmark, and said that while ENTRA1 continues work to finalize arrangements required for project development, NuScale is not standing still. It is strengthening original equipment manufacturer capabilities, deepening supply-chain readiness, and positioning for full-scale production.

His capital message was conservative. The approach, he said, is to stay disciplined on capital, hit the milestones the company can control, and ensure that when commercial agreements are finalized, NuScale can deliver without unnecessary delay or added risk. He said the company is ready with approved technology, proven fuel technology, an engineering and regulatory foundation, strategic partnerships, and a global supply chain. He tied that readiness to a broader demand story: artificial intelligence, data-center growth, industrial energy needs, and energy security, all of which, in his telling, are creating demand for reliable, affordable, carbon-free baseload power.

He also walked through the work that is already underway while ENTRA1 advances customer engagements. NuScale, he said, is advancing detailed engineering, locking in key suppliers, and preparing to support the construction and operating license application process, including for a potential Tennessee Valley Authority project. The licensing team, he said, is already preparing to support that application. He called it familiar ground, because the company holds a Nuclear Regulatory Commission design certification and standard design approvals, and because it completed substantial licensing work on the earlier carbon-free power project. A meaningful portion of that prior effort, he said, is directly reusable for T.V.A. or any other future domestic project, which should compress both schedule and cost relative to a first-time application.

Engineering teams, he added, are drawing on experience from RoPower and other programs. Once an engineering, procurement, and construction contractor is selected, NuScale would support that work under a separate contract covering its proprietary design, keeping the company involved in design integrity while the contractor leads overall project delivery. Further along the timeline, NuScale is also positioning to support operator training, start-up consulting, and fuel-preparation activities in coordination with Framatome. Hopkins was careful to say those are longer-dated opportunities, but that the company is laying the groundwork now, and that many of these steps run in parallel rather than in a single-file sequence.

He also named specific supply-chain moves meant to take long-lead risk off the critical path. Framatome, he said, is completing NuScale fuel design well ahead of customer commitments under a dedicated agreement. Paragon has been awarded a contract to finish production development of safety instrumentation and control systems, with NuScale jointly owning the underlying intellectual property. Across the broader supply base, the company is driving dual or tertiary sourcing on the majority of packages so that no single supplier becomes a constraint. For shareholders, he said, the Doosan investment positions NuScale to execute when orders are secured, with component costs expected to be recovered through the owner's contractual payment schedule under a future original equipment manufacturer agreement.

Hopkins was equally clear that T.V.A. is the immediate priority, but not the only conversation. He said NuScale continues to engage utilities, hyperscalers, and major industrial customers, and that the business model combines ENTRA1's commercial development capabilities with NuScale's approved technology, supply chain, and manufacturing readiness. For shareholders, he said, the opportunity is not simply one project. It is the potential to establish a scalable global original equipment manufacturer business capable of supporting multiple customers and deployments over decades. He also said the company expects to provide further updates as discussions mature into actionable commercial commitments. That last clause is worth holding onto, because the call itself did not convert those discussions into named, dated orders.

The commercial pipeline, though, is still mostly about agreements that have not been signed. The press release said NuScale continues to support its commercial partner, ENTRA1 Energy, in dialogue with the Tennessee Valley Authority on what the company described as the development of the largest commercial nuclear power deployment program in United States history. That is the company's characterization of the opportunity, not a signed, funded order. On the call, Hopkins said the process continues, that the company is optimistic, and that what NuScale can control is building the capacity to execute. He called the move into first article a major milestone in preparation for a project such as T.V.A., because it takes the design into physical hardware and helps derisk the path from engineering to commercial delivery. He also acknowledged that the process has been lengthy.

Hamady later clarified the sequencing, which matters a great deal. A power purchase agreement between ENTRA1 and T.V.A. is not itself the sale of modules. After such a power purchase agreement, the company would expect work on pre-engineering, predelivery services, licensing applications, and other engineering services. The sale of the module would come with an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1. Until those agreements exist, the one point nine billion dollar cash pile and the Doosan first-article work are the tangible evidence, and the T.V.A. opportunity remains a process.

Romania is the other named project, and it is quieter, not clearer. The year-ago revenue was tied to RoPower front-end work that has ended. Asked for an update, Hopkins said there is a new administration in place, that there have been some public announcements, and that NuScale continues dialogue with both RoPower and Nuclearelectrica, one of the major shareholders. He said he had recently sent a request to visit with the current administration to get insight into where the government is headed. Quote, So at this time, that's all we know, end quote.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the official transcript.

George Gianarikas of Canaccord Genuity asked for a timeline on a potential commercial agreement with T.V.A. and on other commercial activity, noting that the procurement of long-lead items would seem to indicate some confidence. Hopkins declined to give a date. He said the process continues, that the company is optimistic, and that first-article production is what NuScale can control while it waits. Gianarikas then asked Hamady how much operating-expense growth investors should expect. Hamady said the company does not provide guidance, discussed keeping operating expenses fairly constant, and later in the call the company and coverage noted that operating expenses had been maintained within a plus or minus five percent band for eight straight quarters. Management also said expenses would be expected to grow once NuScale is engaged with a project, with increased spending spread between operating expenses and cost of goods sold.

Nate Pendleton of Texas Capital Bank and Eric Stine of Craig-Hallum asked about commercial and licensing next steps, including what happens once a project is far enough along to support a construction and operating license application. The answers tracked Hopkins's prepared remarks: NuScale would look at revenues from engineering and related services, and a substantial share of prior licensing work, fifty to sixty percent by management's estimate, could be reused. That reusable work is one of the few quantitative claims on the call about how a first commercial project might be cheaper or faster than a clean-sheet application. It is still an estimate, not a signed schedule.

Christopher Souther of Truist Securities asked Hamady to unpack the operating-expense comparison and the role of strategic investors from Korea and Japan. Hamady noted that some of the work with RoPower had wound down, as reflected in revenue, and used the question to talk about the company's Korean and Japanese strategic relationships as part of the manufacturing and commercialization push, including the Doosan work.

Craig Shere of Tuohy Brothers pressed on when the company could give the Street more formal financial guidance. Hamady said NuScale will be able to give guidance soon, and that the objective is to help the Street understand profitability once an original equipment manufacturer agreement is in place. That is the cleanest guidance-about-guidance comment on the call. It also means today's sixty-five million dollars of quarterly operating expenses should not be lightly turned into a forward earnings model for a company that still has almost no product revenue.

Derek Soderberg of Cantor Fitzgerald asked about the path from a power purchase agreement to actual module production. That is the question that produced Hamady's sequencing clarification: a T.V.A. power purchase agreement would be between ENTRA1 and T.V.A., after which NuScale would expect pre-engineering and licensing work, with module sales arriving only with an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1.

Seth Basham of Wedbush Securities asked first about RoPower, which produced Hopkins's answer about the new Romanian administration, and then about other significant investments needed to move toward full-scale production besides the Doosan work, and the timing of those investments. Hamady's answer was short and clear. Quote, We do not have any other significant investments that we are communicating publicly at this time, end quote.

Hopkins closed by saying that while others remain in early stages of regulatory review, technology development, and fuel qualification, NuScale is advancing toward commercial deployment now. He said the focus is securing customer commitments, achieving manufacturing milestones, converting backlog into revenue, and building a scalable, profitable business. The next chapter, he said, will not be measured simply by milestones achieved, but by revenues generated, projects delivered, and lasting value to shareholders.

On the stock, the immediate read was not a simple punishment for the revenue miss. A TIKR report said NuScale rebounded fourteen percent the following morning after the narrower-than-expected loss, and argued that investors were not trading the stock on quarterly sales. That is one published account of the next-session move, not a closing print I am going to treat as the last word, and later commentary also pointed to lingering uncertainty around the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. process. The fair takeaway is that the market was looking through the near-zero revenue line to the cash position and to whether a commercial agreement is getting closer.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. process, and specifically the two agreements that would actually change the financial model: a power purchase agreement between ENTRA1 and T.V.A., and then an original equipment manufacturer agreement between NuScale and ENTRA1. Until those exist, first-article work is preparation, not a substitute for orders.

Second, whether management begins to give formal margin and profitability guidance after an original equipment manufacturer agreement, as Hamady said it wants to do.

Third, operating expenses and cash use. Sixty-five million dollars of quarterly operating expenses against one point nine billion dollars of liquidity is a long runway if expenses stay roughly flat, and a shorter one if a project start causes spending to step up. Investment income of nineteen point one million dollars this quarter is a cushion, not a business model.

Fourth, conversion of manufacturing milestones into recognized revenue. The Doosan first-article contract, the long-lead inventory of sixty-nine point seven million dollars, and the emergency-core-cooling fabrication work are evidence of a supply chain being stood up. They are not yet evidence of a revenue ramp.

Fifth, RoPower and the new Romanian administration. The last meaningful engineering revenue came from that project, and Hopkins's update was that the company is still waiting for clarity.

Sixth, the difference between a certified design and a sold plant. A seventy-seven megawatt module and a nine hundred twenty-four megawatt twelve-module plant are licensed concepts. The investment case now turns on whether a customer signs, funds, and schedules one.

Let me close with a short recap.

NuScale missed published revenue estimates with only two hundred eighty-one thousand dollars of third-quarter sales, down from eight point two million dollars a year earlier after RoPower front-end work ended, but it beat the main consensus on the loss per share, at eleven cents versus a twelve-cent estimated loss. The company held about one point nine billion dollars of liquidity, kept quarterly operating expenses at sixty-five million dollars, and did not issue formal financial guidance. Management's message was that NuScale has entered physical production through a Doosan first-article contract, while the larger commercial prizes, especially the ENTRA1 and T.V.A. opportunity, remain in process. The official transcript makes the sequencing explicit: a power purchase agreement would not itself be a module sale. The thing to watch is whether those agreements arrive, and whether the first-article work stays on schedule until they do.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.nuscalepower.com/hubfs/Website/Investors/2026/SMR-3Q26-Transcript.pdf?hsLang=en

item.title: Rocket Lab Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Rocket Lab, ticker R-K-L-B. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Rocket Lab released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were Sir Peter Beck, founder and chief executive officer; Adam Spice, chief financial officer; and Murielle Baker, director of corporate and launch communications.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage of the results, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the fourth-quarter outlook, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. It was a mixed quarter in the way Wall Street keeps score, and a strong one in the way the company wants to be judged. Revenue was a record two hundred sixty-seven point eight million dollars, which the release rounded to two hundred sixty-eight million dollars, up seventy-three percent from a year earlier and about thirty-four million dollars higher than the second quarter. That beat both the company's own prior guidance range of two hundred fifty million to two hundred sixty-five million dollars, and published consensus estimates that clustered around two hundred fifty-five to two hundred fifty-seven million dollars. Investing.com put the estimate at two hundred fifty-seven point one seven million dollars. TipRanks used two hundred fifty-seven point two one million dollars. Benzinga used two hundred fifty-five point seven one million dollars.

Earnings missed. The company reported a G.A.A.P. loss of twelve cents a share, compared with an eight-cent loss in the second quarter. Investing.com and TipRanks said the consensus was a loss of seven cents. Benzinga said estimates were for a six-cent loss. The twelve-cent loss missed that cluster. The Motley Fool transcript takeaway said the wider loss was influenced by Iridium transaction costs and debt extinguishment. Operating expenses also ran hot. Non-G.A.A.P. operating expenses were one hundred thirty point two million dollars, above the company's prior guidance range of one hundred twenty-one million to one hundred twenty-seven million dollars. An Investing.com analysis said G.A.A.P. operating expenses were one hundred sixty-nine point three million dollars against guidance of one hundred forty-three million to one hundred forty-nine million dollars, with Neutron development and Iridium deal charges among the drivers.

The backlog is the number Beck put at the center of the story. Total backlog was approximately three point five seven billion dollars, a fifty-two percent sequential increase from about two point four billion dollars at the end of the second quarter. Nearly one billion dollars of that increase came from new launch contracts signed in the third quarter across Electron, HASTE, and Neutron, and the company also signed four hundred seventy million dollars of new Space Systems contracts, up five hundred twelve percent from a year earlier. Year-to-date Space Systems contracts were six hundred eighty-eight million dollars, up three hundred nineteen percent from the same period in twenty twenty-five. The launch backlog rose to one hundred seventeen launches, a new record. Of the current backlog, thirty-two point nine percent is expected to be recognized as revenue within the next twelve months, which means most of the record backlog sits further out.

Beck said, quote, Q three twenty twenty-six was a defining quarter for Rocket Lab, end quote, in the release, and pointed to the combination of record revenue, record backlog, and an end-to-end space strategy in which launch, spacecraft, and components are increasingly sold together. Twelve Rocket Lab-built spacecraft were successfully launched and are now operating, including eight satellite platforms for Globalstar's direct-to-device constellation, twin spacecraft conducting Mars science for NASA, the VICTUS HAZE mission for the United States Space Force, and a spacecraft for Viasat's NASA Communications Services Depot. More than fifty-five spacecraft are now in development and build.

The revenue mix still tilts toward Space Systems. Space Systems revenue was two hundred fourteen point eight million dollars, up thirteen point three percent sequentially, helped by satellite-platform scaling and contributions from recent laser-communications and robotics acquisitions. Launch services revenue was fifty-three point one million dollars, up nineteen percent sequentially, after two additional Electron missions on which full value was recognized at launch. Electron production averaged one rocket every eight work days, which the company said allows it to meet surges in customer demand. Production headcount rose forty percent from the prior quarter, to one thousand seven hundred twenty-eight employees.

Neutron was the strategic center of the launch discussion, and it came with both pricing power and a delay. The company signed eight Neutron launches in the third quarter for approximately five hundred fifteen million dollars, bringing the Neutron backlog to sixteen missions ahead of the rocket's debut. The base launch price on multiple missions signed in the quarter was seventy million dollars, an escalated rate the company tied to tightening global launch supply. An Investing.com analysis said that was up from fifty-five million dollars, a twenty-seven percent increase, and that open slots now start in the twenty thirties. I am treating the seventy million dollar price and the sixteen-mission backlog as company figures, and the comparison with a prior fifty-five million dollar price as published analysis.

The first Neutron launch is now targeted for no earlier than twenty twenty-seven. Critical milestones continue across assembly, integration, testing, and delivery of first-flight hardware to Launch Complex Three. Coverage of the call said first flight slipped after composite voids were found in the first-stage tank, requiring replacement and cryogenic retesting, and that management was not ready to revise its one-three-five launch cadence plan. I will be careful here. The official release uses the "no earlier than twenty twenty-seven" language. The tank-void explanation appears in contemporaneous coverage of the call, and it is one of the first things to confirm in the transcript's technical discussion rather than to over-specify beyond what the company itself put in the release.

Margins were a bright spot. Non-G.A.A.P. gross margin was thirty-eight point four percent, above management's prior guidance range of thirty-five to thirty-seven percent, thanks to favorable product mix and absorption. G.A.A.P. research and development expense was ninety-eight point four million dollars, up sixteen million dollars sequentially, primarily for Neutron Flight One development and engine production. Capital expenditures were thirty-one point one million dollars, including Neutron infrastructure such as the recovery barge the company refers to as the Return on Investment barge.

Cash flow improved sharply, even if free cash flow was not yet positive. G.A.A.P. operating cash flow was a positive seven point two million dollars, compared with a use of eighty-four point one million dollars in the second quarter, driven by milestone payments on satellite programs. Non-G.A.A.P. free cash flow was a use of twenty-three point nine million dollars, an improvement from a use of one hundred ten point one million dollars in the second quarter. Liquidity was four point seven billion dollars, including two point four billion dollars of gross proceeds from an at-the-market equity offering completed in September. That offering fully funded the pending acquisition of Iridium Communications. The company also said it received approval from Iridium lenders to maintain Iridium's credit facility after the transaction, and obtained overwhelming approval from Iridium shareholders. Regulatory approval remains the outstanding item.

Fourth-quarter guidance is for another record revenue quarter, with a profitability outlook that was a bit weaker than some estimates. Rocket Lab expects revenue of two hundred seventy million to two hundred ninety million dollars, or about four point five percent sequential growth at the midpoint. That midpoint of two hundred eighty million dollars is above the analyst consensus Investing.com and TipRanks put near two hundred sixty-five million dollars. G.A.A.P. gross margins are guided to thirty-four to thirty-six percent, and non-G.A.A.P. gross margins to thirty-nine to forty-one percent. G.A.A.P. operating expenses are guided to one hundred sixty-two million to one hundred sixty-eight million dollars, and non-G.A.A.P. operating expenses to one hundred thirty-six million to one hundred forty-two million dollars. Net interest income is guided at forty-five million dollars. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. is guided to a loss of fourteen million to twenty million dollars. TipRanks noted that the consensus adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. estimate was a loss of about twelve point six million dollars, so the guided loss is wider than that estimate. The company also guided to six hundred eighty-one million basic weighted-average common shares outstanding, including about forty-one million Series A convertible participating preferred shares.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

The call drew a long analyst line: Andres Sheppard of Cantor Fitzgerald, Edison Yu of Deutsche Bank, John Godyn of Citigroup, Jan Engelbrecht of Baird, Ronald Epstein of Bank of America, Trevor Walsh of Citizens, Kristine Liwag of Morgan Stanley, Gautam Khanna of T.D. Securities, Andre Madrid of B.T.I.G., Jeff Van Rhee of Craig-Hallum, Michael Leshock of KeyBanc Capital Markets, Erik Rasmussen of Stifel, Anthony Valentini of Barclays, Suji Desilva of Roth Capital, and Ryan Koontz of Needham.

Andres Sheppard of Cantor Fitzgerald asked about the backlog increase and about Neutron pricing. Spice's answer is worth quoting closely. He said, just to be clear, the Neutron pricing isn't going to seventy million dollars, it is at seventy million dollars, and that the company has already put some of that pricing into backlog. That distinction matters. This is not a future price target. It is a current booked price on missions already signed.

John Godyn of Citigroup congratulated the company on reaching one hundred Electron launches faster than Falcon nine did, while noting that Falcon nine later scaled to around one hundred seventy launches a year. Beck said Electron is not a reusable vehicle, and that the big unlock for huge cadence is reusability, even as the factory has already pushed production to a high rate. On a supply-chain follow-up about the large number of satellites in build, Beck said Rocket Lab is so vertically integrated that the things it worries about are different from those of companies that do not control as much of their own supply chain.

Jan Engelbrecht of Baird asked a broader competitive question. Beck said that, fundamentally, two commercial companies have developed a vehicle, brought it to market, and scaled: SpaceX and Rocket Lab. Spice added that he does not think a roughly twenty percent launch growth rate is at risk, given the demand the company has been talking about, and that on HASTE and related hypersonic-test work, the company does not see cancellation risk, describing those programs as pretty bipartisan and long-standing.

Ronald Epstein of Bank of America asked about the tight launch market. Beck said he was hoping someone was not going to ask that question, then said launch capacity is incredibly constrained, and that in many respects Rocket Lab is rooting for everybody because the constraint is industry-wide. Spice said rising prices for Electron are certainly helping, and that getting deposits in for Neutron launches is helping, but that nothing is really going to permanently change the cash profile by itself in the way some investors might hope from price alone.

Trevor Walsh of Citizens asked where development effort is going. Beck said the work has been all around how to increase launch cadence faster, primarily around engines and production. Spice noted that Space Systems, now by far the largest part of the business, is not overly research-and-development intensive, and that the company will continue to invest where it must for Neutron and related launch capability.

Michael Leshock of KeyBanc asked about pad capacity. Beck said there are actually two pads side by side, so capacity is higher than a single-pad image would suggest, because the company can turn launches as people have seen. Suji Desilva of Roth Capital asked a deal-structure question; Spice said it is a tricky question, and that you kind of build the deal you want when it is put in front of you, and that a deal had not been put in front of the company that was enough to take a much different shape. Ryan Koontz of Needham asked about contract quality. Beck said none of these contracts are, in his words, janky contracts with silly things in them, that customers do a lot of due diligence, and that the company has long-standing relationships.

The questions clustered around five topics.

First, whether the backlog is real and how fast it converts. Only thirty-two point nine percent of backlog is expected to come into revenue in the next twelve months, so analysts wanted to understand how much of the three point five seven billion dollars is near-term versus Neutron and later Space Systems work. Management said it felt very good about the state of the backlog, and pointed to the breadth of new launch and spacecraft awards.

Second, Neutron pricing and timing. The seventy million dollar base price and the sixteen-mission backlog were treated as evidence of pricing power in a tight launch market. The offset was the "no earlier than twenty twenty-seven" debut and the work still required on first-flight hardware. Analysts wanted to know whether the delay changes the early flight cadence, and management, according to later coverage, was not ready to rewrite the one-three-five plan on the call.

Third, the Iridium transaction. The deal is financed, lenders have agreed to keep the credit facility in place, and Iridium shareholders have approved it. The remaining gate is regulatory approval. Analysts asked whether that process is on track. Management called progress positive and did not give a date.

Fourth, cost discipline. This quarter's operating expenses came in above guidance, and the fourth-quarter G.A.A.P. operating-expense range of one hundred sixty-two million to one hundred sixty-eight million dollars stays high. That is part of why the earnings per share miss and the wider-than-expected adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. guide weighed on the first reaction, even after a revenue beat and a raised top-line outlook.

Fifth, the end-to-end model: whether launch, spacecraft, and components are truly being pulled through together, and whether new mission classes, including defense-related orbital infrastructure, are becoming real demand or remaining concept-stage.

Edison Yu of Deutsche Bank asked about that more speculative end of the market, including defense-based orbital data centers. Beck said the company has always retained a healthy level of skepticism, but has also been bullish on that category. On a follow-up about what has to happen for the economics to work, he said that for him it is economics, that a number of key things have to happen for those economics to close, and that those key things are extremely difficult. In other words, management is willing to talk about the opportunity, and is not willing to pretend the business case has already closed.

Iridium came up as a financing and process update more than as a new strategic reveal. The company has already funded the pending acquisition through the September at-the-market offering, received lender approval to keep Iridium's credit facility in place, and received overwhelming shareholder approval. Regulatory approval is the remaining advertised gate. Management described progress as positive and did not attach a date. That transaction, if it closes, would add a constellation-operator dimension to a company that has been a builder and a launcher. Until it closes, the four point seven billion dollar liquidity figure already includes the equity that was raised to fund it, and the share count in the fourth-quarter guide already reflects a much larger equity base.

On Neutron timing, the official language remains first launch no earlier than twenty twenty-seven, with first-flight hardware moving to Launch Complex Three. Contemporaneous coverage of the call said composite voids in the first-stage tank required replacement and cryogenic retesting, and that management was not ready to revise a one-three-five early-cadence plan. The seventy million dollar price, already in backlog, is the demand side of that story. The date and the first-flight hardware work are the execution side.

Beck's closing was short. He thanked participants for joining and for the questions, said the company was very pleased with the quarter, and said it looks forward to the next one.

The stock's first move was down, then it recovered. Benzinga said shares were down six point six one percent in after-hours trading Monday, at fifty-four dollars and ninety-seven cents. Investing.com said the stock slumped more than five percent in pre-market Tuesday despite the revenue beat and stronger-than-expected revenue guidance. A later Investing.com note said pre-market was down six point five nine percent, but that the stock had reversed and was trading at sixty dollars and sixty-nine cents, up three point one zero percent, as of twelve thirty-one Eastern on November tenth. The same note pointed out that Rocket Lab had run up nearly eleven percent in the session before the report, so some good news may already have been priced in. TipRanks and others also noted that the fourth-quarter adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. guide was weaker than consensus, which helped explain the negative after-hours reaction.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, fourth-quarter revenue against the two hundred seventy to two hundred ninety million dollar range, and whether gross margins expand as guided, even as the adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss of fourteen to twenty million dollars is wider than some estimates.

Second, Neutron. The first-flight date is now no earlier than twenty twenty-seven, the early backlog is sixteen missions at a higher base price, and the tank and retest work described in coverage is the near-term execution risk.

Third, backlog conversion. A three point five seven billion dollar backlog is only as valuable as the thirty-two point nine percent expected in the next twelve months, plus successful later conversion of Neutron and longer-cycle Space Systems work.

Fourth, Iridium regulatory approval, the last major announced condition after financing and shareholder votes.

Fifth, cost control. Expenses overshot this quarter, and the fourth-quarter operating-expense guide remains elevated. The company has also issued a large amount of equity, including the two point four billion dollar September at-the-market offering, and will have six hundred eighty-one million basic shares in the fourth-quarter share count, including preferred shares.

Sixth, whether positive G.A.A.P. operating cash flow of seven point two million dollars is the start of a pattern, or a milestone-timing quarter, given that non-G.A.A.P. free cash flow was still a use of twenty-three point nine million dollars.

Let me close with a short recap.

Rocket Lab beat on record revenue of about two hundred sixty-eight million dollars, above both its own prior guidance and consensus of roughly two hundred fifty-six million dollars, but missed on a twelve-cent G.A.A.P. loss per share against estimates of about six to seven cents. Backlog jumped fifty-two percent, to about three point five seven billion dollars, after nearly one billion dollars of new launch contracts and four hundred seventy million dollars of Space Systems awards, including eight Neutron missions at a seventy million dollar base price. Fourth-quarter revenue was guided to two hundred seventy million to two hundred ninety million dollars, above consensus, with an adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss of fourteen to twenty million dollars, a bit wider than some estimates. Neutron's debut is now no earlier than twenty twenty-seven, the Iridium deal still needs regulatory approval, and shares fell after hours before recovering the next session. The follow-through is whether the record backlog converts, and whether Neutron and costs stay under control.

Thanks for listening.
