Welcome to this earnings brief for Rocket Lab, ticker R-K-L-B. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Rocket Lab released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were Sir Peter Beck, founder and chief executive officer; Adam Spice, chief financial officer; and Murielle Baker, director of corporate and launch communications.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage of the results, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the fourth-quarter outlook, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. It was a mixed quarter in the way Wall Street keeps score, and a strong one in the way the company wants to be judged. Revenue was a record two hundred sixty-seven point eight million dollars, which the release rounded to two hundred sixty-eight million dollars, up seventy-three percent from a year earlier and about thirty-four million dollars higher than the second quarter. That beat both the company's own prior guidance range of two hundred fifty million to two hundred sixty-five million dollars, and published consensus estimates that clustered around two hundred fifty-five to two hundred fifty-seven million dollars. Investing.com put the estimate at two hundred fifty-seven point one seven million dollars. TipRanks used two hundred fifty-seven point two one million dollars. Benzinga used two hundred fifty-five point seven one million dollars.

Earnings missed. The company reported a G.A.A.P. loss of twelve cents a share, compared with an eight-cent loss in the second quarter. Investing.com and TipRanks said the consensus was a loss of seven cents. Benzinga said estimates were for a six-cent loss. The twelve-cent loss missed that cluster. The Motley Fool transcript takeaway said the wider loss was influenced by Iridium transaction costs and debt extinguishment. Operating expenses also ran hot. Non-G.A.A.P. operating expenses were one hundred thirty point two million dollars, above the company's prior guidance range of one hundred twenty-one million to one hundred twenty-seven million dollars. An Investing.com analysis said G.A.A.P. operating expenses were one hundred sixty-nine point three million dollars against guidance of one hundred forty-three million to one hundred forty-nine million dollars, with Neutron development and Iridium deal charges among the drivers.

The backlog is the number Beck put at the center of the story. Total backlog was approximately three point five seven billion dollars, a fifty-two percent sequential increase from about two point four billion dollars at the end of the second quarter. Nearly one billion dollars of that increase came from new launch contracts signed in the third quarter across Electron, HASTE, and Neutron, and the company also signed four hundred seventy million dollars of new Space Systems contracts, up five hundred twelve percent from a year earlier. Year-to-date Space Systems contracts were six hundred eighty-eight million dollars, up three hundred nineteen percent from the same period in twenty twenty-five. The launch backlog rose to one hundred seventeen launches, a new record. Of the current backlog, thirty-two point nine percent is expected to be recognized as revenue within the next twelve months, which means most of the record backlog sits further out.

Beck said, quote, Q three twenty twenty-six was a defining quarter for Rocket Lab, end quote, in the release, and pointed to the combination of record revenue, record backlog, and an end-to-end space strategy in which launch, spacecraft, and components are increasingly sold together. Twelve Rocket Lab-built spacecraft were successfully launched and are now operating, including eight satellite platforms for Globalstar's direct-to-device constellation, twin spacecraft conducting Mars science for NASA, the VICTUS HAZE mission for the United States Space Force, and a spacecraft for Viasat's NASA Communications Services Depot. More than fifty-five spacecraft are now in development and build.

The revenue mix still tilts toward Space Systems. Space Systems revenue was two hundred fourteen point eight million dollars, up thirteen point three percent sequentially, helped by satellite-platform scaling and contributions from recent laser-communications and robotics acquisitions. Launch services revenue was fifty-three point one million dollars, up nineteen percent sequentially, after two additional Electron missions on which full value was recognized at launch. Electron production averaged one rocket every eight work days, which the company said allows it to meet surges in customer demand. Production headcount rose forty percent from the prior quarter, to one thousand seven hundred twenty-eight employees.

Neutron was the strategic center of the launch discussion, and it came with both pricing power and a delay. The company signed eight Neutron launches in the third quarter for approximately five hundred fifteen million dollars, bringing the Neutron backlog to sixteen missions ahead of the rocket's debut. The base launch price on multiple missions signed in the quarter was seventy million dollars, an escalated rate the company tied to tightening global launch supply. An Investing.com analysis said that was up from fifty-five million dollars, a twenty-seven percent increase, and that open slots now start in the twenty thirties. I am treating the seventy million dollar price and the sixteen-mission backlog as company figures, and the comparison with a prior fifty-five million dollar price as published analysis.

The first Neutron launch is now targeted for no earlier than twenty twenty-seven. Critical milestones continue across assembly, integration, testing, and delivery of first-flight hardware to Launch Complex Three. Coverage of the call said first flight slipped after composite voids were found in the first-stage tank, requiring replacement and cryogenic retesting, and that management was not ready to revise its one-three-five launch cadence plan. I will be careful here. The official release uses the "no earlier than twenty twenty-seven" language. The tank-void explanation appears in contemporaneous coverage of the call, and it is one of the first things to confirm in the transcript's technical discussion rather than to over-specify beyond what the company itself put in the release.

Margins were a bright spot. Non-G.A.A.P. gross margin was thirty-eight point four percent, above management's prior guidance range of thirty-five to thirty-seven percent, thanks to favorable product mix and absorption. G.A.A.P. research and development expense was ninety-eight point four million dollars, up sixteen million dollars sequentially, primarily for Neutron Flight One development and engine production. Capital expenditures were thirty-one point one million dollars, including Neutron infrastructure such as the recovery barge the company refers to as the Return on Investment barge.

Cash flow improved sharply, even if free cash flow was not yet positive. G.A.A.P. operating cash flow was a positive seven point two million dollars, compared with a use of eighty-four point one million dollars in the second quarter, driven by milestone payments on satellite programs. Non-G.A.A.P. free cash flow was a use of twenty-three point nine million dollars, an improvement from a use of one hundred ten point one million dollars in the second quarter. Liquidity was four point seven billion dollars, including two point four billion dollars of gross proceeds from an at-the-market equity offering completed in September. The company also said it received approval from Iridium lenders to maintain Iridium's credit facility after the transaction, and obtained overwhelming approval from Iridium shareholders. Regulatory approval remains the outstanding item.

Fourth-quarter guidance is for another record revenue quarter, with a profitability outlook that was a bit weaker than some estimates. Rocket Lab expects revenue of two hundred seventy million to two hundred ninety million dollars, or about four point five percent sequential growth at the midpoint. That midpoint of two hundred eighty million dollars is above the analyst consensus Investing.com and TipRanks put near two hundred sixty-five million dollars. G.A.A.P. gross margins are guided to thirty-four to thirty-six percent, and non-G.A.A.P. gross margins to thirty-nine to forty-one percent. G.A.A.P. operating expenses are guided to one hundred sixty-two million to one hundred sixty-eight million dollars, and non-G.A.A.P. operating expenses to one hundred thirty-six million to one hundred forty-two million dollars. Net interest income is guided at forty-five million dollars. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. is guided to a loss of fourteen million to twenty million dollars. TipRanks noted that the consensus adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. estimate was a loss of about twelve point six million dollars, so the guided loss is wider than that estimate. item.title: Rigetti Computing Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Rigetti Computing, ticker R-G-T-I. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Rigetti released the numbers on Tuesday, November tenth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call the same day. On the call were Subodh Kulkarni, president and chief executive officer, and Jeffrey Bertelsen, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the full-year outlook, management's technology points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. It was a technology-milestone quarter and a revenue-miss quarter. Third-quarter revenue was one point four million dollars, down from one point nine million dollars a year earlier, because of the timing of system deliveries and customer acceptance milestones. That missed Wall Street badly. Published recaps, including TipRanks and Benzinga, put the consensus near three point five two million dollars, which would make the result a miss of roughly sixty percent. I will not pretend a one point four million dollar quarter was close to that estimate. At the same time, revenue for the first nine months was ten point nine million dollars, compared with five point two million dollars in the first nine months of twenty twenty-five, growth of about one hundred ten percent, and already above the seven point one million dollars Rigetti reported for all of twenty twenty-five. This is a lumpy hardware-and-services business, and one quarter's timing can look nothing like the year-to-date trend.

The company maintained full-year twenty twenty-six revenue guidance of approximately twenty million dollars, assuming customer acceptance of the C-DAC system and associated revenue recognition in the fourth quarter. That assumption is the whole ballgame for the guide. If C-DAC acceptance slips, the twenty million dollar year is at risk. If it happens in the fourth quarter, nine-month revenue of ten point nine million dollars implies about nine point one million dollars in the fourth quarter, a huge step-up from one point four million dollars in the third. That is possible in a milestone business, and it is also a concentrated risk.

On earnings, the G.A.A.P. and non-G.A.A.P. figures tell different stories, and investors should keep them apart. G.A.A.P. net loss was three point one million dollars. Diluted G.A.A.P. loss per share was eight cents, which included a twenty-five point three million dollar non-cash gain from the change in fair value of derivative warrant liabilities. Basic G.A.A.P. loss per share was one cent. Non-G.A.A.P. net loss, which excludes stock-based compensation and those fair-value adjustments, was twenty point five million dollars, or six cents a diluted share. Published recaps said the consensus non-G.A.A.P. loss was about five cents, so the adjusted figure modestly missed. Operating loss widened to thirty-three point two million dollars from twenty point five million dollars a year earlier, reflecting higher research and development. Research and development expense was twenty-five point five million dollars, driven by higher salary costs and work toward large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. Selling, general, and administrative expense was eight point five million dollars, up from five point nine million dollars. Gross margin was sixty-one percent, up from twenty-one percent a year earlier, though management noted that margins vary with contract mix and hardware-revenue timing. A sixty-one percent margin on one point four million dollars of revenue is not yet a scale story.

The balance sheet remains the cushion. Cash, cash equivalents, and available-for-sale investments were four hundred ninety-seven point one million dollars at quarter-end, with no debt. Capital expenditures were forty-two point six million dollars for the first nine months, primarily for dilution-refrigeration capacity and fabrication equipment. Operating cash flow was a use of forty-nine point one million dollars in the first nine months, compared with forty-three point six million dollars a year earlier. The company also signed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to one hundred million dollars of funding under the CHIPS Act, to accelerate research in miniaturized readout electronics and cryogenic capacity. As a condition of the award, Rigetti issued seven point seven million shares of common stock to the department, a minority noncontrolling equity interest. For context on scale, the company used about three hundred thirty-six point four million weighted-average basic shares in the third quarter, according to the earnings release, so the Commerce issuance is dilutive but not transformative by itself. The more important funding fact is the one Bertelsen confirmed: the CHIPS cash is still ahead of the company, not already in the four hundred ninety-seven point one million dollar cash and investment total. On the call, Quinn Bolton of Needham asked whether that one hundred million dollars of cash is on the balance sheet today. Bertelsen said it is not, and that the company will draw down the funds as costs are incurred.

Kulkarni's prepared remarks were mostly about the technology roadmap, not about the revenue miss. The company said its Cepheus-one-one hundred eight-Q system achieved a median two-qubit gate fidelity of ninety-nine point five percent, meeting a performance milestone for its one-hundred-plus-qubit architecture and, in management's view, further validating a chiplet-based approach. The system is built from twelve interconnected nine-qubit chiplets. It also achieved ninety-nine point six percent median two-qubit fidelity on an eighty-qubit sublattice and ninety-nine point seven percent on a fifty-qubit sublattice. Rigetti said its superconducting systems continuously achieve gate speeds of fifty to seventy nanoseconds, which the company describes as about ten thousand times faster than trapped-ion systems and one hundred times faster than neutral-atom systems. Those comparisons are management claims, and I am reporting them as such.

The next official system target is a three-hundred-plus-qubit machine with about ninety-nine point seven percent median two-qubit gate fidelity and gate speeds below sixty nanoseconds by mid-twenty twenty-eight, with a larger qubit count per chiplet, faster readout, and expanded cryogenic capacity. Beyond that, Rigetti continues to target a path toward about one thousand physical qubits, about ninety-nine point nine percent two-qubit fidelity, and gate speeds below fifty nanoseconds within approximately three years. The company believes that combination of scale, fidelity, and speed could provide a platform for demonstrating quantum advantage. Management also said future one-thousand-plus-qubit systems will require a transition to thirty-six-qubit chiplets, up from the current nine-qubit configuration, and a shift from coaxial cables to superconducting flex cables and eventually fiber optics to overcome wiring limits. Rigetti is collaborating with Riverlane on real-time quantum error correction, which it believes is necessary for practical applications.

Kulkarni also spent time on why the company thinks a modular, chiplet-based architecture is the right scaling path. In the Motley Fool takeaway of the call, he said this approach enables higher performance at a lower cost on the path toward systems with thousands and eventually tens of thousands of qubits. That is a long-dated claim, and it is the reason the ninety-nine point five percent fidelity result on a one hundred eight-qubit, twelve-chiplet machine was treated as a validation event, not only as a laboratory footnote. If chiplets can be linked without wrecking fidelity, the company can grow qubit count by adding modules rather than by yielding a single giant chip. If they cannot, the mid-twenty twenty-eight three-hundred-qubit target and the later one-thousand-qubit target get much harder. Krish Sankar's later question about chiplet connections was aimed at exactly that risk.

The wiring roadmap is part of the same scaling problem. Coaxial cables work at today's qubit counts. Management said a move to superconducting flex cables, and eventually fiber optics, is needed to overcome physical wiring limits as the machines grow. Dilution-refrigerator capacity is the other physical constraint, which is why nine-month capital spending of forty-two point six million dollars went largely to refrigeration and fabrication equipment. This is not a software-margin business yet. It is a company spending tens of millions of dollars a year to build the machinery that might, in a few years, support a system that can demonstrate quantum advantage.

The gross-margin jump to sixty-one percent from twenty-one percent deserves the same caution as the G.A.A.P. profit appearance. On one point four million dollars of revenue, mix and the timing of a single hardware acceptance can move the margin enormously. Management said as much. Investors should not annualize sixty-one percent, just as they should not annualize one point four million dollars of quarterly sales, or a three point one million dollar G.A.A.P. net loss that includes a twenty-five point three million dollar warrant gain.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

Kevin Garrigan of Jefferies asked first, and the discussion went to the quarterly timing and to the C-DAC acceptance that sits under the twenty million dollar year. That is the practical financial question. A one point four million dollar quarter is only a problem for the year if the fourth-quarter milestone does not arrive.

Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities asked about the one hundred eight-qubit system and the path to much larger machines. Kulkarni said the one hundred eight-qubit system is already deployed, that only a couple of companies are in that neighborhood, and that, based on the company's data, Rigetti believes it can get to one thousand physical qubits and well beyond that. He also discussed the chiplet approach as a way to reach higher performance at lower cost on the path toward thousands, and eventually tens of thousands, of qubits. Ellis congratulated him and said he looked forward to hearing more.

Gary Mobley of StoneX asked about how customers are actually using the systems, including on the public cloud. Kulkarni said Rigetti's system is one of the most reliable, consistently performing systems available on public clouds right now, and that this gives the company a good vantage point on how customers are using the machines, including people who are still trying to understand what quantum computing can and cannot do, and who are working on applications and algorithm development. He said that ecosystem work matters, because the company does not want to arrive near quantum advantage and only then discover that it needs applications.

Krish Sankar of T.D. Cowen asked about the limits of connecting chiplets. Kulkarni said that as of today the company has limitations coming from connecting chiplets, and that it does not see performance deterioration because it is using an interposer. That is a technical answer with a commercial implication: the modular strategy is only as good as the links between chiplets when the qubit count rises from one hundred eight toward three hundred and then one thousand.

Quinn Bolton of Needham asked about the CHIPS Act funding, including how it will be drawn, and Bertelsen confirmed the one hundred million dollars is not on the balance sheet today and will be drawn down as costs are incurred, quarter by quarter. Bolton also asked about government programs more broadly. Kulkarni pointed to expected initiatives not only in the United States and the United Kingdom, but in other countries, and said Rigetti will participate as it makes sense.

Brian Kinstlinger of Alliance Global asked about go-to-market and customer engagement around the larger systems. Tyler Anderson of Craig-Hallum, and analysts from Cantor Fitzgerald, Rosenblatt Securities, and U.S. Bancorp, also asked questions, including about partnership models for specific roadmap milestones and about how the company plans to share more on error correction and application development as it gets closer to quantum advantage. Kulkarni said investors should definitely expect more discussion of error correction, and also of application development, and that a partnership model is part of how some of the later milestones will be pursued.

He was emphatic that application work cannot wait until the hardware is perfect. Thousands of people, he said, are using the systems every day, many of them trying to understand what quantum computing can and cannot do, and looking at applications and algorithm development. In his view, that is a critical role Rigetti needs to play so that, when the company gets closer to quantum advantage, it does not arrive there and only then say it needs applications. Programming a quantum computer, he said, is fundamentally different from programming a classical computer, so more application and algorithm developers need to come into the ecosystem now. That is a reasonable industry point, and it is also not the same thing as a booked revenue backlog. Exploratory cloud usage can be strategically important and still leave a quarter with only one point four million dollars of recognized sales.

The fidelity numbers themselves need a plain-language translation. A median two-qubit gate fidelity of ninety-nine point five percent on the full one hundred eight-qubit system, and slightly higher figures on smaller sublattices, are the company saying that, more often than not, a two-qubit operation is succeeding at a very high rate. Error correction, and eventually logical qubits, are about turning those still-imperfect physical operations into something reliable enough for useful algorithms. The Riverlane collaboration and the later discussion of error correction are aimed at that next step. The mid-twenty twenty-eight target is not only more qubits. It is also a slightly higher fidelity and faster gates, on a larger chiplet, in a bigger cryogenic plant. Missing any one of those vectors would put the later one-thousand-qubit, ninety-nine point nine percent target further out than the roughly three-year window management is using today.

The stock reacted poorly, as a revenue miss of this size would suggest, though the exact print varies by source. Some recaps said the shares fell about four to five percent after the results. A Motley Fool summary line on the transcript page showed a larger decline, around eight and a half percent. I will not pick a single unofficial last price. The direction was down, and the reason was the third-quarter revenue miss and the fact that the full-year guide now leans so heavily on one fourth-quarter acceptance event. In a milestone business, the market often punishes a slipped or delayed quarter even when management keeps the annual guide unchanged, because the guide itself has become a single-event forecast. That is the position Rigetti is in until C-DAC is accepted.

It is also worth pausing on the share issuance tied to the Commerce Department award. Seven point seven million shares is not a controlling stake, and the company described it as a minority noncontrolling interest, but it is still dilution in exchange for access to up to one hundred million dollars of milestone-based funding that has not yet been received. Combined with the lumpy revenue and the widened operating loss, that is the financial trade-off of the quarter: a stronger technology headline, a weaker revenue print, a still-solid cash account, and a new government partner on the cap table.

The year-to-date numbers should sit beside the quarterly miss, not be used to wave it away. Ten point nine million dollars in nine months, already above last year's full-year revenue, means the business has grown. It also means the remaining nine point one million dollars needed to reach a twenty million dollar year is larger than any quarter Rigetti just reported. Only a successful C-DAC acceptance makes that math look ordinary. Without it, the guide would have to be revisited, and I will not invent a fallback number the company did not give.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, C-DAC customer acceptance and revenue recognition in the fourth quarter, which is the explicit assumption under the twenty million dollar full-year revenue guide.

Second, whether nine-month revenue of ten point nine million dollars plus a successful fourth-quarter milestone actually gets the company to that guide, or whether timing slips again.

Third, cash use against four hundred ninety-seven point one million dollars of cash and investments, with no debt, after a nine-month operating-cash use of forty-nine point one million dollars and forty-two point six million dollars of capital expenditures.

Fourth, the CHIPS Act drawdown, since the one hundred million dollars is milestone-based and not yet on the balance sheet, and since it came with a seven point seven million share issuance to the Commerce Department.

Fifth, the technology path from a one hundred eight-qubit, ninety-nine point five percent fidelity system today to a three-hundred-plus-qubit target by mid-twenty twenty-eight, including chiplet connections, flex cables, cryogenic capacity, and the Riverlane error-correction work.

Sixth, whether application and algorithm work on the cloud systems starts to look like a customer franchise, or remains mostly exploratory. A reliable public-cloud system is an asset. It becomes a financial asset only when usage, acceptances, and contracts show up as revenue in more than one lumpy quarter.

Seventh, dilution and funding mix: the seven point seven million shares issued to the Commerce Department, the still-undrawn CHIPS award, and the cash burn implied by a thirty-three point two million dollar quarterly operating loss and forty-nine point one million dollars of year-to-date operating cash use. The company can fund its roadmap today. It cannot treat the cash pile as inexhaustible if acceptances slip and spending stays high.

Let me close with a short recap.

Rigetti missed third-quarter revenue badly, at one point four million dollars versus published consensus of about three point five million dollars, because of delivery and acceptance timing, even as nine-month revenue rose one hundred ten percent to ten point nine million dollars. The company kept full-year guidance at about twenty million dollars, but only if the C-DAC system is accepted and recognized in the fourth quarter. The G.A.A.P. loss was small only because of a twenty-five point three million dollar warrant gain. The non-G.A.A.P. loss was twenty point five million dollars, or six cents a share, a slight miss versus a five-cent consensus. Cash was four hundred ninety-seven point one million dollars, with no debt. Management's emphasis was a ninety-nine point five percent two-qubit fidelity milestone on the one hundred eight-qubit Cepheus system and a multi-year roadmap toward three hundred and then about one thousand qubits. Shares fell after the miss. The follow-through is almost entirely about whether C-DAC closes in the fourth quarter, and whether the technical milestones stay on the published calendar. If the system is accepted and the revenue is recognized, this quarter's miss will look like a timing hole in a growth year. If it is not, investors will be left with a strong fidelity headline, a four hundred ninety-seven million dollar cash account, and a full-year revenue number that missed the company's own guide. That is a sharp distinction, and it should be knowable when the fourth-quarter results are reported.

Until then, the right way to hold this report is as a technology update with a delayed sales quarter, not as a sudden change in the long-term roadmap, and not as a quarter that already secured the year. The fidelity milestone is real, the revenue miss is real, and the year still depends on one customer acceptance in the fourth quarter. That is a simple, high-stakes test for a lumpy quantum hardware company, and it is the right place to leave the story until the next earnings report arrives early next year, when that acceptance will either be in the results or it will not. Thanks for listening.

It becomes a financial asset only when usage, acceptances, and contracts show up as revenue in more than one lumpy quarter.

Seventh, dilution and funding mix: the seven point seven million shares issued to the Commerce Department, the still-undrawn CHIPS award, and the cash burn implied by a thirty-three point two million dollar quarterly operating loss and forty-nine point one million dollars of year-to-date operating cash use. The company can fund its roadmap today. It cannot treat the cash pile as inexhaustible if acceptances slip and spending stays high.

Let me close with a short recap.

Rigetti missed third-quarter revenue badly, at one point four million dollars versus published consensus of about three point five million dollars, because of delivery and acceptance timing, even as nine-month revenue rose one hundred ten percent to ten point nine million dollars. The company kept full-year guidance at about twenty million dollars, but only if the C-DAC system is accepted and recognized in the fourth quarter. The G.A.A.P. loss was small only because of a twenty-five point three million dollar warrant gain. The non-G.A.A.P. loss was twenty point five million dollars, or six cents a share, a slight miss versus a five-cent consensus. Cash was four hundred ninety-seven point one million dollars, with no debt. Management's emphasis was a ninety-nine point five percent two-qubit fidelity milestone on the one hundred eight-qubit Cepheus system and a multi-year roadmap toward three hundred and then about one thousand qubits. Shares fell after the miss. The follow-through is almost entirely about whether C-DAC closes in the fourth quarter, and whether the technical milestones stay on the published calendar. If the system is accepted and the revenue is recognized, this quarter's miss will look like a timing hole in a growth year. If it is not, investors will be left with a strong fidelity headline, a four hundred ninety-seven million dollar cash account, and a full-year revenue number that missed the company's own guide. That is a sharp distinction, and it should be knowable when the fourth-quarter results are reported.

Until then, the right way to hold this report is as a technology update with a delayed sales quarter, not as a sudden change in the long-term roadmap, and not as a quarter that already secured the year. The fidelity milestone is real, the revenue miss is real, and the year still depends on one customer acceptance in the fourth quarter. That is a simple, high-stakes test for a lumpy quantum hardware company, and it is the right place to leave the story until the next earnings report arrives early next year, when that acceptance will either be in the results or it will not. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Quantum Computing Inc Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Quantum Computing Incorporated, ticker Q-U-B-T, often called Q.C.I. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. The company released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were David Moskowitz, head of investor relations; Yuping Huang, chairman and chief executive officer; and Christopher Bruce Roberts, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's next-day reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the lack of formal guidance, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Revenue jumped, and the loss per share missed. Quantum Computing Incorporated generated nine point five million dollars of third-quarter revenue, compared with three hundred eighty-four thousand dollars a year earlier. That figure also exceeded the nine point two million dollars of revenue the company reported for the entire first half of twenty twenty-six. It beat published estimates. MarketBeat put the consensus at seven point six one million dollars. So this was a clear top-line beat, and a sharp step-up from the company's own recent run rate.

The bottom line went the other way. The company reported a net loss of fifteen point one million dollars, or seven cents a share, compared with net income of two point four million dollars, or one cent a share, a year earlier. MarketBeat said that missed a consensus loss of four cents by three cents. Coverage after the call treated the quarter as a revenue beat and an earnings miss, and the shares gapped down the next session. MarketBeat said the stock opened at six dollars and forty-seven cents, after a prior close of six dollars and eighty-six cents.

The company did not issue formal financial guidance. Roberts was explicit about why. He said the timing of orders and deliveries is difficult to predict, so quarter-to-quarter results are likely to be lumpy, and that the company is not giving guidance at this time. He also said that, over a twelve- to fifteen-month view, management is confident it will have a strong finish to this year and a solid backlog leading into twenty twenty-seven.

Most of the revenue growth came from businesses acquired in the first half of the year. The press release said growth was primarily driven by Luminar Semiconductors, NuCrypt, and NHanced Semiconductors, including photonic components, quantum communications products, and advanced packaging services sold to aerospace, government, and industrial customers. Huang's message was that Q.C.I. is shifting from years of building photonic-based quantum technology to putting those technologies into customers' hands and building a business that can grow sustainably. He said the company has spent years building technology designed for the real world, and that attention is now shifting from what it can build to what it can put to work for customers. That means delivering on commitments and building a business that can grow sustainably. Execution, he said, matters more than ever, and the third-quarter results, in his view, reflect progress in that direction.

Before questions, he came back to a more cautious industry point. He said quantum technology offers tremendous potential, but it is a young industry, and adoption will develop differently across markets and applications. Some customers need photonic technologies today, while others are still exploring what quantum systems can enable as they become more capable and practical. The company, he said, needs to understand those differences and be thoughtful about where it invests. As Roberts outlined, the financial position gives considerable flexibility, particularly in an industry where technology takes time to mature. For Q.C.I., that means advancing the science while building products customers can depend on, growing commercial relationships, improving manufacturing, following through on the roadmap, and being ambitious about what can be achieved while remaining realistic about what it takes to get there.

Gross profit was only four hundred twenty-eight thousand dollars, for a gross margin of four point five percent. That is a thin margin, and management did not pretend otherwise. Roberts said margins remain modest, and that as revenue grows the company sees opportunities to improve manufacturing utilization, increase operating efficiency, and expand margins over time. The company is still in the early innings of integrating acquired factories and filling them.

Operating expenses were twenty-nine point zero million dollars, compared with ten point five million dollars a year earlier. The increase was largely due to higher personnel and related costs from expanded research and development, sales, and marketing, plus about one million dollars of acquisition-related expenses. Interest and other income totaled thirteen point zero million dollars, up from three point five million dollars, mainly from interest on a much larger cash and investment balance. That interest income is a big reason the net loss was not even wider. The press release and the call both make clear that the change from year-ago net income to this quarter's net loss was due largely to higher operating expenses and to smaller mark-to-market gains on a warrant derivative, partly offset by higher revenue and higher interest income.

The balance sheet is the feature that lets the company talk about scale before the margins are healthy. Roberts said Q.C.I. ended the third quarter with approximately one point three billion dollars in cash equivalents and investments, consistent with the end of the second quarter. Total assets were about one point six billion dollars. Total liabilities were forty-seven point seven million dollars. Cash and cash equivalents were one hundred seventy-four point three million dollars, with about one point one billion dollars in investments, and working capital of about nine hundred sixteen point nine million dollars. Management said that liquidity is sufficient to fund operations for at least the next twelve months. Headcount was three hundred thirty employees, up from about three hundred ten at the end of the second quarter.

Contract backlog was thirty-nine point one million dollars, down about two million to three million dollars from the prior quarter, which Roberts attributed to the ordinary difference between contracted orders and recognized revenue. He said backlog typically burns off over twelve to eighteen months, with most of it likely to convert in the next twelve months, but with some more complex products taking longer. That timing variability is also why the company is not guiding quarter by quarter. A backlog that is only about four times this quarter's revenue, and that already declined a little as revenue was recognized, is useful, but it is not a multi-year locked-in book of business. New orders have to keep arriving for the growth to continue.

The first-half comparison is the cleanest way to see the step-up. The company did more revenue in this one quarter than in the first six months of the year combined. That is encouraging, and it is also why a single lumpy quarter should not be extrapolated in a straight line. If a few large aerospace or government deliveries slipped from the third quarter into the fourth, or the other way around, the year could still finish strong, as management expects, without every quarter looking like this one.

On the product side, Huang and the prepared materials emphasized Dirac-three, the company's quantum optimization machine. Capacity was cited at nine thousand nine hundred eighty variables, an increase from previous generations, and the first customer shipment is expected in the fourth quarter of twenty twenty-six. That shipment is one of the few dated product milestones on the call, and it is a useful checkpoint for whether the quantum story is starting to sit beside the acquired photonics revenue, or still mostly behind it. About seventy percent of current revenue is from aerospace and government subcontracts, with a long-term goal of a fifty-fifty commercial split. Getting to that split would require either a lot more commercial work, a change in the government mix, or both, and it will not happen in a single quarter.

The company also pointed to a first pharmaceutical-market collaboration with INmune Bio, a framework agreement with Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar for cloud access to Dirac-three and quantum education, and a benchmark of Dirac-three against the Hexaly classical solver in which management said the quantum system showed better overall performance in time to solution and quality for specific problems. Those are management-reported comparisons and early commercial beachheads, not an independent bake-off I can certify, and not yet a second revenue engine on the scale of the acquired aerospace and government work. They do, however, show how management wants the story to broaden: from components and packaging sold mainly into government supply chains, toward quantum systems and services in new verticals, including pharma and international education and cloud access.

The manufacturing map underneath all of that is still messy, in a way the company itself admits. Eleven facilities in eight states is a lot of footprint for a company that just reported nine point five million dollars of quarterly revenue. The acquisitions were designed to bring in photonics, quantum communications, and advanced packaging, and to speed the Fab Two plan. The test now is whether that footprint gets used more fully, or whether it remains a collection of sites with a four point five percent blended gross margin and one million dollars of leftover acquisition costs in the quarter.

Capital allocation is now a central investor question, because the company has more than a billion dollars to put to work. Roberts said Q.C.I. has earmarked several hundred million dollars for capital expenditure, and that the investment planned for the NHanced Fab Two facility is in the ballpark of seventy million to eighty million dollars. Equipment orders have already begun, and a lot of that spend is expected between now and March thirty-first of next year. He also said the company continues to review deal flow and acquisition opportunities, while wanting enough working capital to ride through periods when raising capital would be highly dilutive. The company has already completed three acquisitions in about eight months.

Huang added that last year's original plan for Fab Two was a greenfield approach, with a later step expected perhaps at the end of twenty twenty-eight, and that the NHanced acquisition has accelerated that roadmap. He said the acquired facilities serve two purposes: supporting the quantum roadmap, including work toward heterogeneous integrated circuits that the team hopes to demonstrate in a twelve- to eighteen-month timeframe, or possibly sooner, and enabling volume production of quantum devices after more than twenty years of research.

Roberts also flagged a risk that did not get a lot of headlines but should be on the list. He said there is a possibility of export restrictions later on, and that I.T.A.R. regulations or other geopolitical factors could complicate future international sales of cutting-edge technology. He also said the bulk of sales and backlog is still domestic, with a few small overseas sales.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt opened with a question that led Roberts into the lumpiness of revenue and awards. Roberts said there is not much to read into a single-quarter backlog change, that backlog was down about two to three million dollars, and that backlog will fluctuate as the difference between contracted orders and recognized revenue. That set the tone for the rest of the call: this is a lumpy, low-volume, technically complex manufacturing business, not a smooth software subscription curve.

Max Michaelis of Lake Street Capital Markets asked what milestones to watch on commercial growth over the next twenty-four months, and what the bigger hurdles are on the manufacturing-scale side. Roberts repeated that the company is not giving guidance because order and delivery timing is hard to predict, that quarters will be lumpy, and that the signs of progress to watch are a strong finish to the year, a solid backlog into twenty twenty-seven, and evidence that a broader range of customers is validating the technology.

Scott Buck of Milan Partners asked how quickly the thirty-nine point one million dollar backlog converts, and about bringing manufacturing operations together. Roberts said the backlog typically converts over twelve to eighteen months, with most of it likely in the next twelve months and some taking longer because the company is building small numbers of very complex products, where a slip of a couple of weeks can move revenue recognition. On manufacturing, he said the company has operations in eight states and eleven facilities, and that the work is more about integrating the company than about a simple site consolidation, deferring some of the detail to Huang.

Nehal Chokshi of Northland Capital Markets also joined the queue, and Kieran McCabe of Cantor asked about the INmune Bio announcement, the first customer in pharma and biotech, and whether a new chief revenue officer signals a push into industries beyond aerospace and defense. Huang said yes, the company is looking at other industries, including biotech and pharma, and that the strategy is both to go deeper within organizations and to spread within those verticals. The Fab Two follow-up is where he explained that NHanced has accelerated a roadmap that had been a later greenfield plan.

Ed Woo of Ascendiant Capital asked how much of the pipeline is U.S. versus international, and about long-term revenue potential. Roberts said the bulk of sales, backlog, and revenue is still domestic, that the company is looking at international opportunities and has made a few small overseas sales, and that he would not over-specify a single long-term market size on the call. That answer sits next to his later comment about possible export restrictions. International expansion is an opportunity and a policy risk at the same time.

Jesse Sockler of B.T.I.G. asked the integration question most directly. He said a lot of the investment world still sees Luminar Semiconductors, NHanced, NuCrypt, and the core business as four separate businesses, and he asked what the first wave of flagship or integrated products looks like, and on what timeline. Huang said the acquired facilities support the quantum roadmap and have already made possible prototypes that could not have been built before the sites were combined. He said the team hopes to demonstrate some heterogeneous integrated circuits in twelve to eighteen months, perhaps sooner, and that after more than twenty years of quantum research the company now has to solve the scalable manufacturing challenge so it can put products into many customers' hands. Sockler's follow-up was about the capital plan for more than a billion dollars of cash. That produced Roberts's seventy to eighty million dollar Fab Two figure and the comment that a lot of the spend will occur by March thirty-first of next year, while the company continues to evaluate equipment needs and acquisition opportunities and wants to avoid raising capital when it would be highly dilutive.

One more point on expectations, because the miss on earnings can be misread. The seven-cent loss is a real miss against a four-cent consensus, but this is not a company that was expected to be profitable. The disappointment is about the pace of spending and the still-thin margin, not about a failed profitable quarter. The encouragement is about the revenue run rate and the cash. Both can be true at the same time, which is why the next few quarters, not this one quarter, will decide how the story is remembered.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether fourth-quarter revenue stays strong enough to support management's comment about a strong finish to the year, including the first Dirac-three customer shipment expected in the quarter, without a formal guide to measure it against.

Second, backlog. Thirty-nine point one million dollars is a real foundation, but it declined by a couple of million dollars this quarter, converts over twelve to eighteen months, and will bounce around as orders and deliveries land.

Third, gross margin. Four point five percent is not a finished manufacturing story. The test is whether utilization and integration lift that margin as the acquired factories scale.

Fourth, spending and dilution risk. The company has about one point three billion dollars of liquidity and is planning seventy to eighty million dollars for Fab Two, plus possible further acquisitions, while still expecting additional losses and elevated operating expenses.

Fifth, whether the acquired businesses start to look like one company, especially if Huang's twelve- to eighteen-month goal for heterogeneous integrated circuits is met, and whether the revenue mix can move from about seventy percent aerospace and government toward a more commercial balance.

Sixth, export and international policy risk, which Roberts raised himself, even though most sales are still domestic.

It is also worth keeping the scale in perspective. Nine point five million dollars is a record quarter for this company, and it is still a small manufacturing business measured against a one point three billion dollar cash and investment account and twenty-nine million dollars of quarterly operating expenses. Interest income of thirteen million dollars is doing a lot of work. If rates fall, or if more of the cash is spent on factories and acquisitions, that cushion shrinks. The acquired photonics, packaging, and communications businesses are what made the revenue step-up possible. They are also why gross margin is only four point five percent and why investors, as Sockler said, still struggle to see one company instead of four. The next few quarters should show whether utilization, integration, and Dirac-three shipments start to change those facts, or whether revenue remains lumpy and the equity story remains mostly about the cash pile and the roadmap.

Let me close with a short recap.

Quantum Computing Incorporated beat on revenue, at nine point five million dollars versus consensus of about seven point six million dollars and versus three hundred eighty-four thousand dollars a year earlier, but missed on a seven-cent loss per share against a four-cent estimated loss. Gross margin was only four point five percent, operating expenses jumped to twenty-nine million dollars, and interest income of thirteen million dollars helped cushion the loss. The company held about one point three billion dollars of cash and investments and a thirty-nine point one million dollar backlog, and it did not issue formal guidance because orders and deliveries are lumpy. Management is steering toward manufacturing scale, a seventy to eighty million dollar Fab Two build, and a first Dirac-three shipment in the fourth quarter. Shares gapped down after the miss on earnings, opening the next session at six dollars and forty-seven cents versus a prior close of six dollars and eighty-six cents, according to MarketBeat. That is a modest gap, not a collapse, but it is a reminder that investors were looking through a record revenue quarter to the seven-cent loss, the thin margin, and the still-unguided outlook. The follow-through is whether the revenue step-up is durable, whether Dirac-three actually ships in the fourth quarter, and whether margins and integration start to catch up with the new scale. If they do, this quarter can look like the start of a commercial manufacturing company. If they do not, it can look like a cash-rich holding company that had one strong delivery quarter after a string of acquisitions.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/09/qc-inc-qubt-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/

Huang added that last year's original plan for Fab Two was a greenfield approach, with a later step expected perhaps at the end of twenty twenty-eight, and that the NHanced acquisition has accelerated that roadmap. He said the acquired facilities serve two purposes: supporting the quantum roadmap, including work toward heterogeneous integrated circuits that the team hopes to demonstrate in a twelve- to eighteen-month timeframe, or possibly sooner, and enabling volume production of quantum devices after more than twenty years of research.

Roberts also flagged a risk that did not get a lot of headlines but should be on the list. He said there is a possibility of export restrictions later on, and that I.T.A.R. regulations or other geopolitical factors could complicate future international sales of cutting-edge technology. He also said the bulk of sales and backlog is still domestic, with a few small overseas sales.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt opened with a question that led Roberts into the lumpiness of revenue and awards. Roberts said there is not much to read into a single-quarter backlog change, that backlog was down about two to three million dollars, and that backlog will fluctuate as the difference between contracted orders and recognized revenue. That set the tone for the rest of the call: this is a lumpy, low-volume, technically complex manufacturing business, not a smooth software subscription curve.

Max Michaelis of Lake Street Capital Markets asked what milestones to watch on commercial growth over the next twenty-four months, and what the bigger hurdles are on the manufacturing-scale side. Roberts repeated that the company is not giving guidance because order and delivery timing is hard to predict, that quarters will be lumpy, and that the signs of progress to watch are a strong finish to the year, a solid backlog into twenty twenty-seven, and evidence that a broader range of customers is validating the technology.

Scott Buck of Milan Partners asked how quickly the thirty-nine point one million dollar backlog converts, and about bringing manufacturing operations together. Roberts said the backlog typically converts over twelve to eighteen months, with most of it likely in the next twelve months and some taking longer because the company is building small numbers of very complex products, where a slip of a couple of weeks can move revenue recognition. On manufacturing, he said the company has operations in eight states and eleven facilities, and that the work is more about integrating the company than about a simple site consolidation, deferring some of the detail to Huang.

Nehal Chokshi of Northland Capital Markets also joined the queue, and Kieran McCabe of Cantor asked about the INmune Bio announcement, the first customer in pharma and biotech, and whether a new chief revenue officer signals a push into industries beyond aerospace and defense. Huang said yes, the company is looking at other industries, including biotech and pharma, and that the strategy is both to go deeper within organizations and to spread within those verticals. The Fab Two follow-up is where he explained that NHanced has accelerated a roadmap that had been a later greenfield plan.

Ed Woo of Ascendiant Capital asked how much of the pipeline is U.S. versus international, and about long-term revenue potential. Roberts said the bulk of sales, backlog, and revenue is still domestic, that the company is looking at international opportunities and has made a few small overseas sales, and that he would not over-specify a single long-term market size on the call. That answer sits next to his later comment about possible export restrictions. International expansion is an opportunity and a policy risk at the same time.

Jesse Sockler of B.T.I.G. asked the integration question most directly. He said a lot of the investment world still sees Luminar Semiconductors, NHanced, NuCrypt, and the core business as four separate businesses, and he asked what the first wave of flagship or integrated products looks like, and on what timeline. Huang said the acquired facilities support the quantum roadmap and have already made possible prototypes that could not have been built before the sites were combined. He said the team hopes to demonstrate some heterogeneous integrated circuits in twelve to eighteen months, perhaps sooner, and that after more than twenty years of quantum research the company now has to solve the scalable manufacturing challenge so it can put products into many customers' hands. Sockler's follow-up was about the capital plan for more than a billion dollars of cash. That produced Roberts's seventy to eighty million dollar Fab Two figure and the comment that a lot of the spend will occur by March thirty-first of next year, while the company continues to evaluate equipment needs and acquisition opportunities and wants to avoid raising capital when it would be highly dilutive.

One more point on expectations, because the miss on earnings can be misread. The seven-cent loss is a real miss against a four-cent consensus, but this is not a company that was expected to be profitable. The disappointment is about the pace of spending and the still-thin margin, not about a failed profitable quarter. The encouragement is about the revenue run rate and the cash. Both can be true at the same time, which is why the next few quarters, not this one quarter, will decide how the story is remembered.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether fourth-quarter revenue stays strong enough to support management's comment about a strong finish to the year, including the first Dirac-three customer shipment expected in the quarter, without a formal guide to measure it against.

Second, backlog. Thirty-nine point one million dollars is a real foundation, but it declined by a couple of million dollars this quarter, converts over twelve to eighteen months, and will bounce around as orders and deliveries land.

Third, gross margin. Four point five percent is not a finished manufacturing story. The test is whether utilization and integration lift that margin as the acquired factories scale.

Fourth, spending and dilution risk. The company has about one point three billion dollars of liquidity and is planning seventy to eighty million dollars for Fab Two, plus possible further acquisitions, while still expecting additional losses and elevated operating expenses.

Fifth, whether the acquired businesses start to look like one company, especially if Huang's twelve- to eighteen-month goal for heterogeneous integrated circuits is met, and whether the revenue mix can move from about seventy percent aerospace and government toward a more commercial balance.

Sixth, export and international policy risk, which Roberts raised himself, even though most sales are still domestic.

It is also worth keeping the scale in perspective. Nine point five million dollars is a record quarter for this company, and it is still a small manufacturing business measured against a one point three billion dollar cash and investment account and twenty-nine million dollars of quarterly operating expenses. Interest income of thirteen million dollars is doing a lot of work. If rates fall, or if more of the cash is spent on factories and acquisitions, that cushion shrinks. The acquired photonics, packaging, and communications businesses are what made the revenue step-up possible. They are also why gross margin is only four point five percent and why investors, as Sockler said, still struggle to see one company instead of four. The next few quarters should show whether utilization, integration, and Dirac-three shipments start to change those facts, or whether revenue remains lumpy and the equity story remains mostly about the cash pile and the roadmap.

Let me close with a short recap.

Quantum Computing Incorporated beat on revenue, at nine point five million dollars versus consensus of about seven point six million dollars and versus three hundred eighty-four thousand dollars a year earlier, but missed on a seven-cent loss per share against a four-cent estimated loss. Gross margin was only four point five percent, operating expenses jumped to twenty-nine million dollars, and interest income of thirteen million dollars helped cushion the loss. The company held about one point three billion dollars of cash and investments and a thirty-nine point one million dollar backlog, and it did not issue formal guidance because orders and deliveries are lumpy. Management is steering toward manufacturing scale, a seventy to eighty million dollar Fab Two build, and a first Dirac-three shipment in the fourth quarter. Shares gapped down after the miss on earnings, opening the next session at six dollars and forty-seven cents versus a prior close of six dollars and eighty-six cents, according to MarketBeat. That is a modest gap, not a collapse, but it is a reminder that investors were looking through a record revenue quarter to the seven-cent loss, the thin margin, and the still-unguided outlook. The follow-through is whether the revenue step-up is durable, whether Dirac-three actually ships in the fourth quarter, and whether margins and integration start to catch up with the new scale. If they do, this quarter can look like the start of a commercial manufacturing company. If they do not, it can look like a cash-rich holding company that had one strong delivery quarter after a string of acquisitions.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/09/qc-inc-qubt-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/
