Author: Intuitive Machines
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Intuitive Machines, ticker L-U-N-R, often said as Lunar. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. The company published the numbers on Thursday, November twelfth, twenty twenty-six, before the market opened, and held its conference call at eight thirty in the morning, Eastern Time.

A note up front, because it shapes everything that follows. As of the time this script was written, later that same morning, a public transcript of the call was not yet available. I checked the usual places, including Motley Fool's earnings-call transcript pages, and it had not been posted. So this is not a recap of the live question-and-answer session, and I will not invent analyst questions or management answers. The brief is built from the company's press release and related eight-K filing, plus contemporaneous coverage, published consensus estimates, and the early stock reaction.

Here is the headline. Intuitive Machines reported record quarterly revenue of two hundred sixty-nine point three million dollars. The precise figure in the filing is two hundred sixty-nine million, three hundred forty-eight thousand dollars, compared with fifty-two point four million dollars in the same quarter a year earlier, more than a fivefold increase, or about four hundred fourteen percent. The company also reported a much narrower generally accepted accounting principles, or G.A.A.P., net loss, positive adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, which I will call adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A., and its first distinctly positive free-cash-flow quarter of the year. Contracted backlog at September thirtieth was one billion, eight hundred sixty-six point eight million dollars, up from two hundred thirteen point one million dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five.

Those results beat the published Wall Street estimates, though the exact consensus numbers differ a little by source. Investing.com and MarketBeat both put the consensus near a ten-cent loss and revenue of about two hundred forty-five point seven to two hundred forty-five point nine million dollars, while a twenty-four seven Wall Street recap used a slightly different consensus, a loss of about eleven cents and revenue of about two hundred forty-seven point six million dollars. Published forecasts clustered around a loss of about ten to eleven cents a share and revenue of roughly two hundred forty-six to two hundred forty-eight million dollars. On either reading, revenue came in clearly above the estimates, and the loss per share was much smaller than expected.

The share count matters when you hear that two-cent loss. Weighted-average shares outstanding in the quarter were about one hundred seventy-three point four million, up from about one hundred seventeen point eight million a year earlier. Net loss attributable to Class A common shareholders was four point two million dollars, or two cents a share, compared with seven point zero million dollars, or six cents a share, a year earlier. The company's overall net loss, before allocating results to noncontrolling interests, was three point four million dollars, compared with ten point zero million dollars a year ago.

Chief Executive Officer Steve Altemus framed the quarter as a proof point, not just a beat. In the press release he said, quote, In the third quarter, we delivered record financial performance across the board. These results are an important proof point in our transformation from a company that advanced the state of lunar exploration into a next-generation space prime developing and integrating the technology, infrastructure and services that enable customers to achieve their differentiated missions across space, end quote.

That transformation shows up clearly in the revenue mix. Product revenue, which the company ties to satellite production, was two hundred fifteen point one million dollars in the third quarter. A year earlier, product revenue was zero. Service revenue was fifty-four point one million dollars, up modestly from fifty-one point zero million dollars. Grant revenue was negligible, at ninety-two thousand dollars. In other words, most of the year-over-year jump is not a sudden boom in the old lunar-services business. It is the satellite-production line, which arrived with the January twenty twenty-six acquisition of Lanteris, the former Maxar satellite factory, and which the company says is now contributing at scale.

There is a useful year-to-date wrinkle in that mix. For the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, total revenue was six hundred sixty-two point two million dollars, compared with one hundred sixty-five point three million dollars a year earlier. Product revenue for those nine months was five hundred twenty-three point four million dollars, again compared with zero the year before. Service revenue, though, was lower year to date, at one hundred thirty-two point nine million dollars versus one hundred sixty-three point eight million dollars. The older services book has not been the engine of this year's growth.

Gross profit, which the company described as record gross margin, was sixty-nine million dollars, or twenty-six percent of revenue. The filing supports that rounding: revenue minus cost of revenues was about sixty-nine point three million dollars, before depreciation and amortization, which the company reports on a separate line. Management said that margin was driven by a larger contribution from the satellite-production business, higher volume, and net favorable one-time program adjustments, including estimate-at-completion adjustments and other cost adjustments. That last point is important. The company itself flags those program adjustments as part of the margin story, so the twenty-six percent figure should not be treated as a proven run rate until later quarters show whether it holds without those one-time items.

Profitability below the gross-profit line is more mixed, and that is where a casual reading of the two-cent loss can mislead. Operating loss actually widened. The company lost thirty-four point two million dollars from operations in the quarter, compared with a fifteen point four million dollar operating loss a year earlier. Total operating expenses were three hundred three point six million dollars, up from sixty-seven point nine million dollars. Cost of revenues was two hundred million dollars. Depreciation and amortization jumped to thirteen point two million dollars from eight hundred fifteen thousand dollars, which is what you would expect after a large manufacturing acquisition. Research and development rose to seven point five million dollars, and general and administrative expense, excluding depreciation and amortization, jumped to eighty-two point nine million dollars from sixteen point three million dollars.

So how does a wider operating loss become a much narrower net loss, and then a positive adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. figure? The gap is in the adjustments and in other income. Total other income, net, was thirty point nine million dollars in the quarter. Almost all of that came from non-cash fair-value items: a thirty point zero million dollar gain from the change in the fair value of warrant liabilities, and a three point six million dollar gain from the change in the fair value of contingent consideration liabilities. Interest income was three point zero million dollars, interest expense was four point five million dollars, and there was no income-tax expense in the quarter. After those items, net loss was three point four million dollars.

Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A., a non-G.A.A.P. measure, was positive eight point three million dollars, compared with a loss of thirteen point two million dollars in the year-ago quarter. The company's reconciliation starts from that three point four million dollar net loss and adds back depreciation and amortization of thirteen point two million dollars, interest expense of four point five million dollars, acquisition and integration costs of nine point six million dollars, non-recurring legal expense of ten point three million dollars, and share-based compensation of ten point six million dollars, while subtracting interest income of three point zero million dollars and the warrant and contingent-consideration gains. That math lands at eight point three million dollars of adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A.

Two things are worth holding onto from that bridge. First, the G.A.A.P. net-loss improvement was helped in a major way by those warrant and contingent-consideration gains, which can move around with the share price and with valuation assumptions, and which are not cash from selling satellites or flying missions. Second, adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. adds back real cash costs the company treats as non-recurring or transactional, including about nine point six million dollars of acquisition and integration costs and about ten point three million dollars of non-recurring legal expense, which the filing does not spell out in any detail. For the first nine months, adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. was still slightly negative, at three point zero million dollars, compared with a loss of forty-five point one million dollars a year earlier, so the full-year goal of a positive figure still depends on a solid fourth quarter.

Cash flow is the other record the company emphasized, and it deserves the same kind of careful reading. In the third quarter, cash from operations was a positive sixty-six point two million dollars, compared with seven point two million dollars used in the year-ago quarter. Purchases of property and equipment were thirty-two point seven million dollars, which the press release rounded to thirty-three million dollars. That left free cash flow of about thirty-three point five million dollars, which the company rounded to a positive thirty-three million dollars. The company defines free cash flow as operating cash flow minus those equipment purchases.

For the first nine months, the picture is still negative. Operating activities used forty-five point seven million dollars, purchases of property and equipment were sixty-six point six million dollars, and free cash flow was a use of one hundred twelve point three million dollars, compared with a use of thirty-three point zero million dollars in the first nine months of twenty twenty-five. This was a strong cash quarter inside a year that, through September, had still consumed a lot of cash.

The quarterly cash-flow statement also shows why a single good quarter should be handled carefully. Contract liabilities increased by seventy-four point one million dollars, accounts payable and accrued expenses increased by fifty-four point two million dollars, and other liabilities increased by ninety-eight point seven million dollars, all of which helped operating cash. On the other side, contract assets increased by sixty-nine point zero million dollars, other assets increased by seventy-two point nine million dollars, and inventory used another ten point seven million dollars. There was also a provision for credit losses of nine point five million dollars, a non-cash add-back in the operating-cash reconciliation. Working-capital timing was a large part of the quarter's cash generation, alongside the operating result itself.

The balance sheet got much larger, which is what you would expect after buying a satellite factory and a ground-station business. Total assets were two point two four billion dollars at September thirtieth, up from seven hundred fifty-seven point two million dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five. Cash and cash equivalents were four hundred sixty-three point eight million dollars, down from five hundred eighty-two point six million dollars at year-end. Restricted cash was another thirteen point two million dollars, so cash plus restricted cash was four hundred seventy-seven point zero million dollars.

The cash decline from year-end is not a mystery. In the first nine months, the company spent four hundred sixty-four point nine million dollars on acquisitions, net of cash acquired, including seventeen point eight million dollars in the third quarter, and raised five hundred eleven point nine million dollars from securities issuance year to date, including ninety-eight point one million dollars in the third quarter, before transaction costs of thirteen point three million dollars. Long-term debt was little changed, at three hundred thirty-six point nine million dollars, and warrant liabilities were fifty-one point four million dollars.

You can also see the new operating shape of the company on the balance sheet. Inventory was seventy point six million dollars, compared with zero at the end of twenty twenty-five. Contract assets and trade receivables were both far above their year-end levels of about twelve million dollars, at one hundred twenty point three million and one hundred thirteen point five million dollars, respectively. There is a new non-current line for orbital receivables of two hundred eight point two million dollars. Property and equipment, net, rose to three hundred twenty-six point seven million dollars, while intangible assets and goodwill rose to two hundred seventy-four point nine million and four hundred six point seven million dollars. Current contract liabilities were two hundred ninety-three point five million dollars, accounts payable and accrued expenses were one hundred thirty-nine point two million dollars, and a new pension and postretirement-benefits liability of forty-three point zero million dollars likely arrived with an acquired business.

Now to the number the company put at the center of its outlook: backlog. Contracted backlog at September thirtieth was one billion, eight hundred sixty-six point eight million dollars, which the press release rounded to a record one point nine billion dollars, up from two hundred thirteen point one million dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five. The company said the increase of about one point six five billion dollars includes six hundred twelve point eight million dollars of acquired Lanteris backlog, thirty-one point seven million dollars from the Goonhilly acquisition, and one point seven seven billion dollars in new awards, partly offset by six hundred sixty-two point two million dollars of revenue already recognized and by ninety-four point seven million dollars of adjustments, primarily from descoping the remaining Power Propulsion Element contract and a rideshare contract tied to the I M four mission. The backlog is much larger, but it is not a straight climb. Some previously counted work has been cut back.

The new awards, the company said, were driven mainly by a multi-satellite program supporting three commercial satellites, the Space Development Agency's tranche-three tracking layer, the Accelerated Missile Defense Tranche Three constellation, a Jet Propulsion Laboratory instrument program known as Eagle V-S-W-I-R, and Hartford, two I M three hundred series platforms for a national security space application. It also cited new or expanded work on the I M five and I M six missions, the Near Space Network contract, and other awards.

For the third quarter itself, the press release said the company booked four hundred fifty million dollars of new awards and Goonhilly acquired backlog, driven primarily by the A.M.D.T. three constellation, the Eagle V-S-W-I-R work, and the Hartford platforms. That figure includes the acquired Goonhilly backlog, so it is not entirely organic bookings.

Two important awards landed after the quarter closed, in the fourth quarter, and they should not be confused with already booked third-quarter backlog. First, Intuitive Machines said it was awarded as a vendor on NASA's next-generation Commercial Lunar Payload Services two contract, often called C.L.P.S. two. That is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract, or I.D.I.Q., with a ceiling of ten billion dollars and a five billion dollar option, designed to support more capable cargo missions at greater frequency. A ceiling is not the same thing as funded work. Being named a vendor creates a path to future task orders. It does not mean ten billion dollars has been added to backlog or to revenue.

Second, also in the fourth quarter, the company said it contracted with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory for Falcon Radar, an Earth-observation mission that will study clouds and convection from space. The release does not give a contract value for that award.

The company also closed the Goonhilly Earth Station and Comsat acquisition, which it said expands its space-to-ground data-services network.

On the operating calendar, Altemus pointed to the next missions. He said the company remains laser focused on I M three along with its first Altus-one lunar satellite, which remains on track for a planned launch in the March and April timeframe, and that the emphasis will be to scale execution, accelerate growth, and convert contracted backlog into revenue through repeatable production and reliable customer delivery. The press release also said the company has accelerated plans for the Near Space Network cislunar constellation, with Altus-two through Altus-five to deploy together in twenty twenty-eight on a NASA-provided launch vehicle. I will stay with that wording. The NASA-provided vehicle is what the company attached to the later Altus satellites in twenty twenty-eight. The March and April launch window is what it attached to I M three and Altus-one as it looks toward twenty twenty-seven.

That may also be a shift from what management had said after the second quarter, at least on timing. On the second-quarter call, according to the Motley Fool transcript of that earlier call, Altemus had described Mission Three as scheduled in a January-through-March launch window on a SpaceX Falcon nine. Today's release speaks of a planned launch in the March and April timeframe. Without this morning's transcript, that may be a modest window update, or simply a shorter way of talking about the same plan.

Now, guidance. The company said it expects full-year twenty twenty-six revenue of nine hundred twenty million to nine hundred fifty million dollars, and positive adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. for the full year. The press release states those figures as the outlook. It does not, in so many words, say the company is raising or lowering prior guidance.

The comparison still matters, and the sources do not all describe it the same way. On the second-quarter call, management had guided to a wider range of nine hundred million to one billion dollars of twenty twenty-six revenue, also with positive full-year adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. Today's range sits inside that earlier band, with the low end twenty million dollars higher and the high end fifty million dollars lower. In plain terms, the company narrowed the range, lifted the floor, and cut the ceiling. Investing.com described the new outlook as a raise relative to an analyst consensus of nine hundred nineteen point eight million dollars, not as a raise of the company's own prior range, while twenty-four seven Wall Street described the outlook as kept intact, which does not match the wider second-quarter range.

You can also back into what that implies for the fourth quarter, without treating it as a formal fourth-quarter guide, because the company did not give one. Nine-month revenue is already six hundred sixty-two point two million dollars, so the fourth quarter would need about two hundred fifty-eight million dollars to reach the low end of the full-year range, or about two hundred eighty-eight million dollars to reach the high end. The third quarter, at two hundred sixty-nine point three million dollars, sits inside that implied band. The fourth quarter does not require a dramatic further step-up from the third quarter to make the guide, but it also does not leave a lot of room to fall short.

The early stock reaction was strong. Intuitive Machines shares closed on Wednesday, November eleventh, at twelve dollars and eighteen cents, according to Yahoo Finance. After the results came out Thursday morning, Investing.com, in a report published at eight oh two Eastern, said the shares were up eleven point two five percent in pre-market trading. A later Yahoo Finance pre-market quote, time-stamped at eight fifty-six Eastern, showed the stock at thirteen dollars and ninety-one cents, up fourteen point two zero percent from Wednesday's close. Those are pre-market prints, not a regular-session close, and they can move quickly.

Because there is no public transcript yet, I also cannot give you a true account of the analyst question-and-answer session, or management's live answers on backlog conversion, funding, one-time margin adjustments, legal expense, cash-flow timing, or whether larger awards are still at the authority-to-proceed stage. Those were live issues after the second quarter, when chief financial officer Pete McGrath talked about the timing of contract definitization as the main variable in the revenue range. That is context from the prior call, not a report of what was said this morning. If a transcript is published later, that is the place to pick up those answers rather than guessing at them now.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, fourth-quarter revenue against that implied band of about two hundred fifty-eight to two hundred eighty-eight million dollars, and whether full-year adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. actually turns positive after a nine-month loss of three point zero million dollars.

Second, the quality of the margin. Twenty-six percent gross profit is a standout number, but management already said it included net favorable one-time program adjustments, including estimate-at-completion changes. The next couple of quarters will show whether that margin is durable.

Third, cash flow after this quarter's working-capital swing. Free cash flow was positive by about thirty-three million dollars in the quarter and still negative by one hundred twelve point three million dollars year to date, while cash on hand of four hundred sixty-three point eight million dollars is still substantial but lower than at year-end after the acquisition spending.

Fourth, backlog conversion, and the difference between a headline backlog of one point eight seven billion dollars and actual funded work. The company has already taken ninety-four point seven million dollars of descoping adjustments, and it has not, in this release, broken out how much of the remaining backlog is fully funded or how much it expects to turn into revenue this year versus later. Until the transcript or the coming ten-Q provides that, the size of the backlog should be weighed alongside those gaps.

Fifth, the C.L.P.S. two vendor award. The ten-billion-dollar ceiling with a five-billion-dollar option is a large number, and it is central to the company's lunar-infrastructure story. The thing to watch is not the ceiling. It is whether, and when, NASA places actual task orders, and at what value.

Sixth, execution on the missions already on the calendar. I M three and Altus-one are the near-term operational catalysts, with a planned launch in the March and April timeframe as the company turns into twenty twenty-seven, and Altus-two through Altus-five planned to go up together in twenty twenty-eight on a NASA-provided launch vehicle. Mission success, schedule, and cost will matter at least as much as any one quarter's beat.

Seventh, integration. This is now a company with a satellite factory, a growing ground network after Goonhilly and Comsat, a much larger share count, and a heavier balance sheet. The story Altemus is telling is that Intuitive Machines has become a next-generation space prime, not only a lunar-lander company, and the open question is whether production, margins, and cash conversion can keep up.

Intuitive Machines' third quarter was a clear beat on revenue and on the loss per share, with record revenue of two hundred sixty-nine point three million dollars, a G.A.A.P. loss of two cents a share, positive adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. of eight point three million dollars, positive quarterly free cash flow of about thirty-three million dollars, and backlog of one billion, eight hundred sixty-six point eight million dollars. The growth is overwhelmingly in product, or satellite-production, revenue after the Lanteris deal. The official full-year outlook is now nine hundred twenty to nine hundred fifty million dollars of revenue, with positive adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A., and the shares jumped in Thursday pre-market trading by about eleven to fourteen percent, depending on the timestamp of the quote.

The caveats sit right beside those records. The narrower G.A.A.P. loss was helped by large non-cash fair-value gains, the twenty-six percent gross margin included favorable one-time program adjustments, operating loss widened, and year-to-date free cash flow is still negative. A public transcript of this morning's call was not yet available, so this brief cannot cover the analyst question-and-answer session. When that transcript is out, the useful follow-up is what management said about backlog conversion, funding, margins, cash timing, and the launch plans.

Thanks for listening.

item.title: IonQ Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for IonQ, ticker I-O-N-Q. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. IonQ released the numbers on Thursday, November fifth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were Hanley Donofrio, vice president of investor relations; Niccolo de Masi, chairman and chief executive officer; and Inder Singh, chief operating officer and chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage of the results, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the raised outlook, management's main points, notable analyst questions from the transcript, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. IonQ reported record quarterly revenue of one hundred seventy-three point eight million dollars, up three hundred thirty-six percent from a year earlier. Management called it the strongest quarter in the company's history and the sixth consecutive record quarter. That figure beat published Wall Street estimates by a wide margin. Investing.com said the consensus revenue estimate was one hundred forty-one point seven one million dollars. A Zacks recap on Yahoo Finance said the result surpassed the consensus mark by about nineteen percent. On earnings, the picture depends on which measure you use. G.A.A.P. earnings were one dollar and forty-two cents a share, compared with a loss of three dollars and fifty-eight cents a year earlier, but that profit was driven by a large non-cash warrant gain. Adjusted earnings, the figure most estimates focus on, were a loss of twenty-nine cents a share. Investing.com said that beat a consensus loss of thirty-one cents. Zacks put the consensus at a loss of thirty cents. Either way, it was a modest beat on the adjusted loss, and a large beat on revenue.

The company also raised its full-year twenty twenty-six revenue guidance to five hundred five million to five hundred fifteen million dollars, from a previous range of four hundred fifty million to four hundred sixty million dollars. The company said that earlier range had been announced at its September Investor Day, according to the Zacks recap. The midpoint of the new range, five hundred ten million dollars, sits well above the analyst consensus Investing.com and Zacks both put near four hundred fifty-five million dollars. IonQ also raised its expectation for year-over-year growth in quantum computing revenue to one hundred ten percent, from a previous target of one hundred percent.

Chief Executive Officer Niccolo de Masi opened by framing the quarter as proof that IonQ is entering a new phase of growth. He said the company has built a quantum platform spanning computing, networking, sensing, and security, supported by vertically integrated manufacturing, and that the focus is now on translating those advantages into broader customer adoption, commercial scale, and long-term shareholder value. He said, quote, Our third quarter results are proof of our strategy in action, end quote. He also said third-quarter revenue of one hundred seventy-three point eight million dollars, quote, reflects increasing demand for our quantum technologies and the benefits of our vertically integrated quantum manufacturing capabilities through SkyWater, end quote, in the earnings release.

The revenue mix shows how much the story has changed. The IonQ Platform segment, which covers the company's quantum products, delivered ninety point three million dollars, up one hundred twenty-seven percent from a year earlier. De Masi called that revenue scale a record for the reporting quantum industry in its own right, and said the quarter was especially strong in quantum computing, with new contracts signed around the world for the company's sixth-generation Superion two hundred fifty-six systems. He said IonQ has sold out all of its two hundred fifty-six capacity in twenty twenty-seven.

The other half of the quarter came from SkyWater. Foundry services contributed eighty-three point five million dollars. That reflects about two months of operations after the acquisition closed at the end of July. The earnings release said revenue from non-IonQ quantum customers at SkyWater was up more than thirty percent year over year, and that the company had launched SkyWater Quantum Solutions. De Masi said SkyWater is home to what he called the industry's most advanced and diverse quantum manufacturing capabilities, and that revenue from within the quantum ecosystem grew as the company added new customers and expanded with existing ones.

Singh, on the financial review, said the results exceeded even the company's own internal modeling, driven by strength across the board, and that closing SkyWater lets IonQ offer customers a vertically integrated company, not just a platform company. Remaining performance obligations, or R.P.O., the contracted revenue not yet recognized, stood at one point two billion dollars, including six hundred eighty-nine million dollars from the IonQ Platform and four hundred seventy-nine million dollars from SkyWater. In the quarter, IonQ signed two hundred ninety million dollars of new contracts in the IonQ Platform segment, of which one hundred eighty million dollars was attributed to quantum computing systems.

Several of those awards were named. A Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency sensing contract was valued at twenty-eight million dollars for the delivery of twenty-five next-generation atomic clocks, with a thirty million dollar option for one hundred additional units. A contract with S.D.T. in South Korea was valued at thirty-three million dollars for a Superion two hundred fifty-six system and a quantum networking memory solution. Florida International University signed a twenty-five million dollar contract for a Superion two hundred fifty-six system. A deal with Congruity three sixty was valued at eight point two million dollars, focused on post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution. Management also said about forty percent of IonQ Platform segment revenue in the quarter came from customers buying more than one solution.

Profitability is where the beat needs a careful reading. G.A.A.P. net income attributable to IonQ was five hundred sixty-four million dollars, or one dollar and forty-two cents a share. That result was driven primarily by an eight hundred ninety-six million dollar non-cash gain from the mark-to-market valuation of warrants. Those gains can swing with the share price and with valuation assumptions. They are not cash from selling systems or foundry work. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A., a non-G.A.A.P. measure, was a loss of one hundred thirty-three point six million dollars. Singh said that figure reflected a heavy concentration of acquisition and integration investment in the quarter. The company recognized about forty million dollars of one-time general and administrative expenses related to the SkyWater acquisition. Operating expenses were six hundred six point nine million dollars on a G.A.A.P. basis, and three hundred six point six million dollars on a non-G.A.A.P. basis. Research and development investment was four hundred twenty-five million dollars year to date, with ninety-six point eight million dollars of non-G.A.A.P. research and development spending in the third quarter. Zacks noted that the adjusted loss of twenty-nine cents was wider than a year-ago adjusted loss of seventeen cents, even as it beat this quarter's consensus.

The balance sheet is a central part of the story. Cash, cash equivalents, and investments were one point seven billion dollars as of September thirtieth. After a two billion dollar equity offering that closed on October sixteenth, pro forma cash was three point seven billion dollars. Management has described IonQ as the best-capitalized pure-play quantum company on that measure. The offering was priced at a premium to the share price, according to the call takeaways. That capital is meant to fund the research roadmap and the integration of a larger manufacturing footprint, but it also means shareholders have already funded a substantial increase in the cash pile.

On guidance, the raise is the main official message. Full-year twenty twenty-six revenue is now expected at five hundred five million to five hundred fifteen million dollars, and quantum computing revenue is expected to grow one hundred ten percent year over year. The company did not, in the materials I used, give a formal full-year adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. range. What Singh did say is important for the fourth quarter. He indicated that the S and P Global Capital I.Q. estimate of a negative one hundred twenty-seven million dollars of adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. for the fourth quarter was not unreasonable. That would be a somewhat narrower loss than the third quarter's one hundred thirty-three point six million dollar adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. deficit, but it is still a deep loss. The company is telling investors that record revenue and a guidance raise are arriving alongside heavy spending and integration costs, not instead of them.

Management's strategic points clustered around four themes.

First, Superion two hundred fifty-six demand and manufacturing. De Masi said IonQ has sold out its two hundred fifty-six capacity for twenty twenty-seven, and that new contracts for those systems were signed globally. The company also said a Superion two hundred fifty-six system will be the first on-premise quantum computer at NVIDIA's Accelerated Quantum Research Center, integrating the system with A.I. supercomputing infrastructure.

Second, a milestone with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA. IonQ said it is the only trapped-ion company to advance to Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, with a potential program value of up to three hundred million dollars. That is a selection and a potential value, not recognized revenue.

Third, the security franchise. IonQ said it is extending its quantum security platform by acquiring Elisity, a company it described as helping customers identify vulnerabilities, enforce zero trust, and provide cryptographic agility as they prepare for the quantum era. The Motley Fool summary of the call said the Elisity deal nearly doubled the company's quantum security customer base, adding about one hundred enterprise deployments to about one hundred twenty-five customers from the I.D. Quantique business. I am using that as a description of what was reported from the call, not as a separately audited customer count.

Fourth, a push toward eventual profitability, even as the current quarter's adjusted loss is large. Singh said September marked his one-year anniversary in the operating role, and that plotting a path for profitable growth is now a priority. He said some products will get there faster than others, and that the company will look across the portfolio when it allocates capital. Operationally, he pointed to monthly and quarterly business reviews, pricing strategy, deal-desk reviews, sales productivity, and merger integration. He was direct about overlap. Quote, With SkyWater and our other acquisitions, we run more back office systems and sites than we need, end quote. He said that is an example of where the company will turn its focus in twenty twenty-seven and look at its site strategy, and that it may consider tying compensation to profitability initiatives as it enters twenty twenty-seven.

Now to the question-and-answer session, using only what is on the Motley Fool transcript.

Vivek Arya of Bank of America opened with a question that led Singh and de Masi into quantum security. Singh said that a quarter or two earlier, security had become more and more prevalent in customer conversations, and that an executive order and other events had made it clearer to large enterprises and governments that classical cybersecurity is not enough, including against a future quantum computer. He said IonQ has assembled a quantum cybersecurity business. De Masi added that he had met with a number of world leaders at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting earlier that week, and that security is seen as the foundation for trusting communications, systems, and networks. He said that, on a combined basis, IonQ has a differentiated software and hardware platform.

Jill Moore of Morgan Stanley, as the analyst was introduced on the call, asked about the NVIDIA announcement and what it means that IonQ systems will be in NVIDIA's research center. The follow-up was whether that deployment is next year, and whether more specific timing had been given. Management discussed the research-center placement as a way to put a Superion two hundred fifty-six system alongside A.I. supercomputing infrastructure. I will stay with what was clearly stated in the release and remarks: the system is planned for NVIDIA's Accelerated Quantum Research Center, and the analyst was asking for tighter timing.

Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities congratulated management on the momentum and followed up on the comment about a busy twenty twenty-seven, noting the company's track record of strong contract signings. He then asked Singh about the path to profitability and the emphasis on back office next year. That exchange is where the site-consolidation and compensation comments sit. Singh used the question to repeat that integration and a tighter operating footprint are twenty twenty-seven work, not a claim that the fourth quarter will already look like a leaner company.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt congratulated the company on DARPA Stage C and on selling out Superion two hundred fifty-six capacity. He asked whether the math on the related slide is as simple as price times units, whether prices are similar across customers, and whether preferred customers would be first in line for later, larger systems, including a ten-thousand-qubit class machine. He also asked for the status of Superion two hundred fifty-six on the bench. The questions themselves tell you what investors are trying to model: sold-out capacity is only as valuable as price, mix, and delivery timing. Management discussed those points in terms of demand and preferred access, without turning the call into a formal price list in the excerpts I am relying on.

Robert Aguanno, asking for Quinn Bolton at Needham and Company, asked two practical questions: what the SkyWater acquisition looks like now that it is closed, and what feedback and process look like in Stage C of the DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. Those are the execution questions behind the strategic headlines. Closing a foundry deal and advancing a government benchmarking program are not the same as converting either one into durable, high-margin revenue.

Gary Mobley of StoneX shifted the discussion away from hardware sales and asked for performance measures on cloud access or revenue from already deployed systems. His follow-up was whether selling out Superion two hundred fifty-six capacity through twenty twenty-seven creates an impediment to further sales. That is a real tension. A sold-out production slot can be a sign of demand, or a cap on near-term incremental bookings, or both. It is one of the cleaner things to watch in coming quarters: whether new signings continue, slip into later years, or shift toward other products in the portfolio.

Tyler Anderson of Craig-Hallum, asking for Richard Shannon, pressed on manufacturing capacity and on making systems that use microwave and electronic controls, then followed up on cryptographic agility and post-quantum cryptography, including the Elisity angle. The manufacturing question matters because SkyWater is supposed to be the answer to scale. The security question matters because management is asking investors to value a multi-product platform, not only computer sales.

Troy Jensen of Cantor Fitzgerald asked de Masi about the pace of future acquisitions, then asked Singh to break down the two hundred ninety million dollars of incremental IonQ Platform remaining performance obligations. Singh had already said one hundred eighty million dollars was systems. Jensen asked about the remaining one hundred ten million dollars, and whether that was primarily the sensing wins, security, or other products. Singh said the remainder came from across the rest of the portfolio, pointed to sensing and security, and said customers are starting the journey with one product and then moving to another. That is the multi-product thesis in a single answer. It is also a reminder that a large share of the new contracted value is already understood as system sales, and that the rest is a blend rather than a single second engine.

De Masi's closing remarks repeated the platform argument. He said IonQ recognized early that customers' most consequential challenges demand more than a single quantum point solution, which is why the company expanded into networking, sensing, and security. He again cited the figure that more than forty percent of the quarter's IonQ segment revenue came from customers buying more than one solution. He said that as the company scales, shared technology, manufacturing, and customer relationships should strengthen each part of the business, and that he expects IonQ, in the coming years, to approach a scale that will support structural profitability.

The stock reaction came in two stages, and the sources do not all use the same timestamp. Investing.com, writing after the Thursday release, said shares were up three percent in after-hours trading. A Zacks recap said the shares gained five point two percent in the after-market session. Then, on Friday, TipRanks reported that IonQ shares surged twenty-three point four two percent, closing at thirty-two dollars and sixty-two cents. That Friday move was the larger, clearer reaction. TipRanks also noted that the stock was still down about twenty-seven percent year to date even after Friday's jump, and that several analysts maintained Buy ratings while cutting price targets, including names that had just been on the call, such as Bank of America's Vivek Arya and B. Riley's Craig Ellis. I am mentioning those target cuts only as later published research, not as something said on the call itself.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether fourth-quarter revenue stays on a path that makes the new five hundred five to five hundred fifteen million dollar full-year range achievable, and whether the adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss narrows toward the neighborhood of the one hundred twenty-seven million dollar fourth-quarter estimate Singh said was not unreasonable.

Second, SkyWater integration. The foundry contributed eighty-three point five million dollars in a partial quarter, and it also contributed a forty million dollar one-time expense and a broader overlap in systems and sites that Singh said will be a twenty twenty-seven focus. The question is how quickly the foundry becomes a durable, profitable manufacturing advantage rather than a cost and complexity story.

Third, conversion of the one point two billion dollars of remaining performance obligations, and of the two hundred ninety million dollars of new IonQ Platform contracts signed in the quarter. Sold-out Superion two hundred fifty-six capacity for twenty twenty-seven is a demand signal. It is also a delivery and timing risk.

Fourth, the mix between system sales and the rest of the platform. One hundred eighty million dollars of the new contracted value was systems. The remaining one hundred ten million dollars, and the forty percent multi-product revenue share, are the evidence for the networking, sensing, and security strategy.

Fifth, the named programs that are still more catalyst than cash: DARPA Stage C, with a potential value of up to three hundred million dollars; the NVIDIA research-center deployment; the Elisity security acquisition; and the clock, university, and networking contracts already announced.

Sixth, the path to what de Masi called structural profitability. The company is well capitalized, at three point seven billion dollars of pro forma cash after the October offering, and it is still investing heavily, with a one hundred thirty-three point six million dollar adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss this quarter and hundreds of millions of dollars of research spending year to date. The next several quarters will show whether the profitability program Singh described is visible in the run rate, or still mainly a twenty twenty-seven talking point.

Let me close with a short recap.

IonQ beat published estimates with record third-quarter revenue of one hundred seventy-three point eight million dollars, against consensus of about one hundred forty-two million dollars, and an adjusted loss of twenty-nine cents a share, a modest beat versus a consensus loss of about thirty to thirty-one cents. G.A.A.P. earnings of one dollar and forty-two cents a share were driven by a large non-cash warrant gain and should not be read as operating profit. The company raised full-year twenty twenty-six revenue guidance to five hundred five million to five hundred fifteen million dollars, from four hundred fifty million to four hundred sixty million dollars, and lifted its quantum computing growth target to one hundred ten percent. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. remained a deep loss, at one hundred thirty-three point six million dollars, after concentrated integration spending, including about forty million dollars of one-time SkyWater costs. Management pointed to sold-out Superion two hundred fifty-six capacity for twenty twenty-seven, a one point two billion dollar backlog of remaining performance obligations, and three point seven billion dollars of pro forma cash. Shares jumped sharply on Friday after a smaller Thursday after-hours gain. The follow-through to watch is whether that demand converts cleanly, and whether the losses start to narrow as the company turns from building a platform to running one.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/06/ionq-ionq-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/

Management pointed to sold-out Superion two hundred fifty-six capacity for twenty twenty-seven, a one point two billion dollar backlog of remaining performance obligations, and three point seven billion dollars of pro forma cash. Shares jumped sharply on Friday after a smaller Thursday after-hours gain. The follow-through to watch is whether that demand converts cleanly, and whether the losses start to narrow as the company turns from building a platform to running one.

item.title: Fervo Energy Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Fervo Energy, ticker F-R-V-O. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Fervo released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call the same day. On the call were Paxton Bentzinger, senior director of corporate development and investor relations; Timothy Latimer, co-founder and chief executive officer; and David Ulrey, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates. I will cover the results against expectations, the updated spending outlook, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. This was Fervo's first quarter with commercial operations, and the financials still look like a construction company more than like a power producer. The company declared commercial operation at Cape Station Phase One, GeoBlock One, on September thirtieth, ahead of the contractual commercial operation date. The first GeoBlock is a thirty-three megawatt unit, and it contributed only a single day of commercial operation in the quarter. Revenue was one hundred sixteen thousand dollars. The earnings release also shows fifty-five thousand dollars of revenue in the year-ago quarter, and two hundred ninety thousand dollars for the first nine months of twenty twenty-six.

That revenue line slightly missed some published estimates. Seeking Alpha said G.A.A.P. earnings of a seven-cent loss beat by two cents, while revenue of twelve one-hundredths of a million dollars missed by three one-hundredths of a million dollars, which implies a consensus near one hundred fifty thousand dollars. TipRanks, citing The Fly, said the seven-cent loss was in line with a seven-cent consensus. I am not going to force those two earnings comparisons into a single official number. What is fair to say is that revenue was still tiny, as one day of commercial operation would suggest, and that the per-share result was either in line or a modest beat, depending on the estimate source, at a seven-cent net loss attributable to common stockholders.

The net income line can confuse if you stop at the first figure. Fervo reported net income of eleven point seven million dollars, but a net loss attributable to common stockholders of twenty point eight million dollars, or seven cents a share. The Motley Fool takeaway noted that the per-share loss included fourteen million dollars of non-cash stock-based compensation. Net income reflected fifteen point four million dollars of interest income and two items the company called non-recurring: an eleven point eight million dollar non-cash gain on interest-rate swaps, and a twenty-nine point nine million dollar tax benefit from tax credits earned as Cape Phase One assets were placed in service. Operating loss was forty-three point seven million dollars. General and administrative expense was thirty-nine point four million dollars, up from twenty-seven point four million dollars in the second quarter, reflecting higher stock-based compensation, public-company costs, and headcount growth. Employees numbered three hundred six at quarter-end, up from two hundred sixty-one in the second quarter, primarily in operations and construction.

In other words, the company made money on interest, a swap mark-to-market, and tax credits, while the operating business was still a sizable loss, and common stockholders still showed a loss. That is a first-power quarter, not a run-rate earnings quarter.

The spending and liquidity figures are the ones that will shape the next year. Capital expenditures were two hundred fifty-six point seven million dollars in the third quarter, compared with two hundred twenty-six point five million dollars in the second quarter, primarily at Cape Station. Fervo expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of about four hundred fifty million to five hundred million dollars, bringing second-half twenty twenty-six spending to seven hundred million to seven hundred fifty million dollars. That is a reduction from the prior second-half range of eight hundred fifty million to nine hundred million dollars, which the company attributed to more efficient spending timelines, not to a smaller project. Unrestricted cash and cash equivalents were one point nine billion dollars, or about one billion, nine hundred sixteen million dollars on the balance sheet. Current and long-term debt totaled three hundred one point six million dollars.

On revenue guidance, the company was conservative in a specific way. It said it continues to anticipate fourth-quarter twenty twenty-six revenue in line with prior expectations, and that this will be the first full quarter of revenue from Cape Station. Revenue in twenty twenty-seven, it said, remains unchanged from prior expectations. The release did not restate the dollar amounts of those prior expectations, so I will not invent them. The official message is that the first-power milestone did not cause a change in the company's previously given revenue outlook, while the second-half capital-expenditure range came down.

Latimer's strategic message was much larger than one hundred sixteen thousand dollars of sales. In the release he said Cape Station reached first power and contractual commercial operation, and that Fervo also signed what it believes is the largest enhanced geothermal power purchase agreement to date, with Google, creating a pathway to scaling the partnership to nearly a gigawatt. Quote, With commercial operations underway and significant demand for our technology, we are focused on delivering the remaining Phase One GeoBlocks on schedule and building toward geothermal as a reliable, always-on, low-cost source of power, end quote.

GeoBlock One, at thirty-three megawatts, is operating in line with expectations for production and power delivered under its power purchase agreement, the company said. GeoBlock Two has achieved grid sync and is in its early operations phase, delivering test energy to the grid. GeoBlock Three is mechanically complete and in cold commissioning. GeoBlocks Two and Three remain on schedule and are expected to achieve commercial operation by January first, twenty twenty-seven, which would complete Cape Station Phase One at about one hundred megawatts from the first three GeoBlocks. Management also said it expects a fifty percent improvement in commissioning speed from GeoBlock One to GeoBlock Three.

The Google agreement is the backlog event of the quarter. It is a fifteen-year, grid-connected, take-or-pay contract for three hundred ninety-six megawatts, with first power expected in mid-twenty twenty-eight. Fervo is also committed to offering Google an option to expand offtake by about six hundred megawatts, which would bring the total partnership to nearly one gigawatt. In connection with the agreement, Fervo progressed construction across Cape Station GeoBlocks Four through Eleven, now referred to as Cape Google Four Hundred, which are expected to provide about four hundred megawatts of power under the Google contract beginning in twenty twenty-eight. The Motley Fool takeaway of the call put the expected total investment for Cape Google Four Hundred at two point two billion dollars through twenty twenty-eight. Installed cost targets cited on the call were five thousand five hundred dollars per kilowatt for that project, with a long-term goal of three thousand dollars per kilowatt. Phase One, the first three GeoBlocks, was cited at seven thousand dollars per kilowatt, including shared infrastructure and capitalized interest. Those cost figures are management targets and reported Phase One costs, not a guarantee of future costs.

With the Google agreement, Fervo now has one thousand fifty-four megawatts of capacity under binding power purchase agreements, up about sixty percent from the second quarter, representing approximately eleven point nine billion dollars in contracted revenue. The early development pipeline rose to fifty-four point seven gigawatts from forty-eight point six gigawatts, and land holdings rose to six hundred seventy thousand acres from six hundred fifty thousand acres. An updated heat-initially-in-place study by DeGolyer and MacNaughton, an independent consulting firm, supported about eight point four gigawatts of capacity potential at Cape Station, nearly double a prior estimate of four point three gigawatts, based on deeper drilling results. The company was also selected for two potential Department of Energy awards totaling about twenty million dollars, including funding for appraisal wells in Idaho and Nevada. Drilling for GeoBlocks Four through Eleven was eighteen percent complete, using four H and P Flex Three rigs.

Safety got a brief but specific mention. The company cited a ten one-hundredths total recordable incident rate, and one million hours worked by the facility construction crew without a recordable incident.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

The analysts included Derek Podhaizer of Piper Sandler, Chris Dendrinos of R.B.C. Capital Markets, David Anderson of Barclays, Dylan Nassano of Wolfe Research, Joseph Osha of Guggenheim Securities, Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies, Justin Clare of Roth Capital Partners, Jeff Grampp of Northland Capital Markets, Sean Milligan of Needham and Company, and Jed Dorsheimer of William Blair.

Derek Podhaizer of Piper Sandler and other early questioners went at Phase One execution: whether GeoBlocks Two and Three remain on track for January first, twenty twenty-seven, how the first days of commercial operation at GeoBlock One have compared with the power purchase agreement, and whether commissioning is actually getting faster. Management's public answers stayed with the release. GeoBlock One is operating in line with expectations. Two is in early operations after grid sync. Three is mechanically complete and in cold commissioning. The company is pointing to a fifty percent commissioning-speed improvement by GeoBlock Three, which, if it holds, is one of the more important operating claims on the call, because the Google build is a repeatable-block story. Grid sync on GeoBlock Two is a meaningful intermediate step. It means the plant is already delivering test energy, not only standing complete in the yard.

Chris Dendrinos of R.B.C., David Anderson of Barclays, and Jeff Grampp of Northland asked, in various forms, about the drilling and surface-facility program that has to feed GeoBlocks Four through Eleven. Eighteen percent of that drilling was complete at quarter-end, with four H and P Flex Three rigs at work. That is still early in a two-point-two-billion-dollar project through twenty twenty-eight. The fourth-quarter capital-expenditure range of four hundred fifty million to five hundred million dollars tells you the spend is about to accelerate, which is consistent with a project that has just moved from first power and a new offtake agreement into a heavier construction phase.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies, Justin Clare of Roth, and others pressed on costs and capital. They wanted to know why second-half capital expenditures were cut to seven hundred million to seven hundred fifty million dollars from eight hundred fifty million to nine hundred million, and whether that was slippage or efficiency. The company's stated reason is more efficient spending timelines, not a smaller project, which is a favorable explanation if it holds and a problem if the spend simply moves later. They also asked about the jump from a seven-thousand-dollar-per-kilowatt Phase One cost to the five-thousand-five-hundred-dollar target for Cape Google Four Hundred, and then to a three-thousand-dollar long-term goal, and about the two point two billion dollar investment figure through twenty twenty-eight. Those questions are the right ones. The first three blocks include shared infrastructure and capitalized interest, so the starting cost should be the high-water mark if the learning curve is real. The later blocks are supposed to show scale benefits. A one point nine billion dollar cash position against three hundred one point six million dollars of debt gives Fervo the ability to fund this build, but the spending rate in the fourth quarter will be several times this quarter's revenue, which is still measured in thousands of dollars, not billions.

A third cluster went to the Google contract and backlog quality. The contract is take-or-pay and fifteen years, which is strong contract structure if the plant is on time. Analysts asked about the six hundred megawatt expansion option, about mid-twenty twenty-eight first power, and about how much of the eleven point nine billion dollars of contracted revenue is the Google deal versus earlier offtake. Management's emphasis was that this is, in its view, the largest enhanced geothermal power purchase agreement to date, and that it creates a path to a nearly one-gigawatt partnership if the option is exercised. An option is not a second signed contract, and I will keep that distinction.

Joseph Osha of Guggenheim, Jed Dorsheimer of William Blair, and others went to the resource estimate and to earlier project performance. The Cape Station resource study nearly doubling, to eight point four gigawatts, is a large number, and the fact that it was completed by DeGolyer and MacNaughton gives it more weight than an internal sketch. Even so, heat initially in place is not the same thing as permitted, contracted, and financed megawatts. The current binding book is one thousand fifty-four megawatts. The early-stage pipeline is fifty-four point seven gigawatts. Those are very different categories. Separately, Latimer discussed performance at the Project Red pilot, including an observation that after a period of stable temperature, production temperature declined. That is a technical risk worth keeping in view, because enhanced geothermal is being sold as always-on, repeatable baseload, and reservoir behavior over time is part of the underwriting. First-day performance at GeoBlock One is encouraging. It is not a multi-year production history.

A fifth cluster went to permitting and policy, including whether anything in the company's growth plans depends on federal permitting legislation sometimes discussed as the BAAJA. Latimer's answer, as reported on the call, was that nothing in the go-forward expectations relies on that legislation, that prior guidance has been based on the company's own expectations for federal permitting timelines, and that if such legislation passed, both geothermal and transmission provisions would be additive, because they could improve the regulatory backdrop and permit timelines. He said Fervo stays keenly focused on it as a potential catalyst, even though the growth plans do not rely on it.

A take-or-pay contract is worth a brief plain-language explanation, because it is central to why the Google backlog number is so large. Under a take-or-pay agreement, the buyer pays for a specified amount of energy whether or not it takes every megawatt-hour. That shifts volume risk toward the offtaker, provided the plant is actually on and delivering within the contract's terms. It does not eliminate construction risk, schedule risk, or reservoir risk on Fervo's side. The eleven point nine billion dollar contracted-revenue figure assumes those plants get built and perform. The three hundred ninety-six megawatt contract, the mid-twenty twenty-eight first-power date, and the two point two billion dollar investment plan are the work that has to happen before that revenue is real.

The company also scheduled an investor open house at Cape Station for Thursday, November nineteenth, twenty twenty-six, with a tour of the site, including the drill rig and power plant. That is a useful reminder of where this story is now. It is a field visit, not an earnings-model quarter. One hundred sixteen thousand dollars of revenue was a rounding error next to two hundred fifty-six point seven million dollars of quarterly capital expenditure, and the fourth quarter is guided to almost twice that spend. The financial story for the next many quarters will be cash, schedule, and cost per kilowatt, not quarterly sales.

On the stock, published reports after the release described a sharp initial bounce, including one account of a more than twenty-six percent surge, followed by a softer pre-market tone as some analysts cut or adjusted price targets. I am not going to treat a single unofficial print as a close. The important point is that investors were reacting to first power and the Google contract, not to the tiny revenue line, and that the reaction was not one-directional once the spending and timeline details were digested.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether GeoBlocks Two and Three actually reach commercial operation by January first, twenty twenty-seven, completing a one-hundred-megawatt Phase One, and whether commissioning really is faster on the later blocks.

Second, the first full quarter of Cape Station revenue in the fourth quarter, against the company's prior revenue expectations, which it reaffirmed but did not restate in dollars in the release.

Third, fourth-quarter capital expenditures of four hundred fifty million to five hundred million dollars, and whether the lower second-half range holds.

Fourth, cost progress from seven thousand dollars per kilowatt on Phase One toward five thousand five hundred dollars on Cape Google Four Hundred, and, much later, the three-thousand-dollar long-term goal.

Fifth, execution on the Google plant: mid-twenty twenty-eight first power, a two point two billion dollar investment through twenty twenty-eight, and whether the six hundred megawatt option ever becomes a signed expansion.

Sixth, reservoir performance, including the Project Red temperature observation, and whether the doubled eight point four gigawatt Cape resource estimate begins to show up in additional contracted offtake, not only in a study.

Seventh, cash use against one point nine billion dollars of unrestricted cash and three hundred one point six million dollars of debt, as hiring, public-company costs, and construction all rise. General and administrative expense already jumped to thirty-nine point four million dollars from twenty-seven point four million dollars in the second quarter, and headcount rose by forty-five people, mostly in operations and construction. That is what a newly public builder looks like when it is staffing a multi-gigawatt pipeline. It is also a cost line that can keep growing even if the next GeoBlocks come in on schedule. The twenty million dollars of potential Department of Energy awards for appraisal drilling in Idaho and Nevada, and the additional twenty thousand acres of land, are modest next to Cape Station, but they are how a fifty-four point seven gigawatt early-stage pipeline starts to become a second geography, not only a single-site story in Utah.

If Phase One reaches one hundred megawatts on January first, investors will have a full winter of operating data before Google's mid-twenty twenty-eight first power. That operating data, plus the fourth-quarter spend, will say more than this quarter's one-day revenue figure ever could.

Let me close with a short recap.

Fervo reached first commercial operation at Cape Station on September thirtieth, but third-quarter revenue was only one hundred sixteen thousand dollars, a slight miss versus some estimates, with a seven-cent net loss to common stockholders that was either in line or a modest beat, depending on the source. The operating loss was still forty-three point seven million dollars, and reported net income was helped by interest income, a swap gain, and a tax-credit benefit. The company cut its second-half capital-expenditure range to seven hundred million to seven hundred fifty million dollars, reaffirmed prior fourth-quarter and twenty twenty-seven revenue expectations, and signed a three hundred ninety-six megawatt, fifteen-year take-or-pay agreement with Google that lifted binding contracted capacity to one thousand fifty-four megawatts and contracted revenue to about eleven point nine billion dollars. GeoBlocks Two and Three are aimed at commercial operation by January first, twenty twenty-seven. The follow-through is whether first power turns into a repeatable, lower-cost build, on schedule, for the much larger Google project, and whether the next two GeoBlocks meet the January first commercial-operation date that would complete Phase One. If they do, Fervo can start to be judged as an operator as well as a builder. If they slip, the eleven point nine billion dollar backlog will look further away than it does today.

That is the test from here. Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/09/fervo-energy-frvo-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/

Author: Fervo Energy

They also asked about the jump from a seven-thousand-dollar-per-kilowatt Phase One cost to the five-thousand-five-hundred-dollar target for Cape Google Four Hundred, and then to a three-thousand-dollar long-term goal, and about the two point two billion dollar investment figure through twenty twenty-eight. Those questions are the right ones. The first three blocks include shared infrastructure and capitalized interest, so the starting cost should be the high-water mark if the learning curve is real. The later blocks are supposed to show scale benefits. A one point nine billion dollar cash position against three hundred one point six million dollars of debt gives Fervo the ability to fund this build, but the spending rate in the fourth quarter will be several times this quarter's revenue, which is still measured in thousands of dollars, not billions.

A third cluster went to the Google contract and backlog quality. The contract is take-or-pay and fifteen years, which is strong contract structure if the plant is on time. Analysts asked about the six hundred megawatt expansion option, about mid-twenty twenty-eight first power, and about how much of the eleven point nine billion dollars of contracted revenue is the Google deal versus earlier offtake. Management's emphasis was that this is, in its view, the largest enhanced geothermal power purchase agreement to date, and that it creates a path to a nearly one-gigawatt partnership if the option is exercised. An option is not a second signed contract, and I will keep that distinction.

Joseph Osha of Guggenheim, Jed Dorsheimer of William Blair, and others went to the resource estimate and to earlier project performance. The Cape Station resource study nearly doubling, to eight point four gigawatts, is a large number, and the fact that it was completed by DeGolyer and MacNaughton gives it more weight than an internal sketch. Even so, heat initially in place is not the same thing as permitted, contracted, and financed megawatts. The current binding book is one thousand fifty-four megawatts. The early-stage pipeline is fifty-four point seven gigawatts. Those are very different categories. Separately, Latimer discussed performance at the Project Red pilot, including an observation that after a period of stable temperature, production temperature declined. That is a technical risk worth keeping in view, because enhanced geothermal is being sold as always-on, repeatable baseload, and reservoir behavior over time is part of the underwriting. First-day performance at GeoBlock One is encouraging. It is not a multi-year production history.

A fifth cluster went to permitting and policy, including whether anything in the company's growth plans depends on federal permitting legislation sometimes discussed as the BAAJA. Latimer's answer, as reported on the call, was that nothing in the go-forward expectations relies on that legislation, that prior guidance has been based on the company's own expectations for federal permitting timelines, and that if such legislation passed, both geothermal and transmission provisions would be additive, because they could improve the regulatory backdrop and permit timelines. He said Fervo stays keenly focused on it as a potential catalyst, even though the growth plans do not rely on it.

A take-or-pay contract is worth a brief plain-language explanation, because it is central to why the Google backlog number is so large. Under a take-or-pay agreement, the buyer pays for a specified amount of energy whether or not it takes every megawatt-hour. That shifts volume risk toward the offtaker, provided the plant is actually on and delivering within the contract's terms. It does not eliminate construction risk, schedule risk, or reservoir risk on Fervo's side. The eleven point nine billion dollar contracted-revenue figure assumes those plants get built and perform. The three hundred ninety-six megawatt contract, the mid-twenty twenty-eight first-power date, and the two point two billion dollar investment plan are the work that has to happen before that revenue is real.

The company also scheduled an investor open house at Cape Station for Thursday, November nineteenth, twenty twenty-six, with a tour of the site, including the drill rig and power plant. That is a useful reminder of where this story is now. It is a field visit, not an earnings-model quarter. One hundred sixteen thousand dollars of revenue was a rounding error next to two hundred fifty-six point seven million dollars of quarterly capital expenditure, and the fourth quarter is guided to almost twice that spend. The financial story for the next many quarters will be cash, schedule, and cost per kilowatt, not quarterly sales.

On the stock, published reports after the release described a sharp initial bounce, including one account of a more than twenty-six percent surge, followed by a softer pre-market tone as some analysts cut or adjusted price targets. I am not going to treat a single unofficial print as a close. The important point is that investors were reacting to first power and the Google contract, not to the tiny revenue line, and that the reaction was not one-directional once the spending and timeline details were digested.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether GeoBlocks Two and Three actually reach commercial operation by January first, twenty twenty-seven, completing a one-hundred-megawatt Phase One, and whether commissioning really is faster on the later blocks.

Second, the first full quarter of Cape Station revenue in the fourth quarter, against the company's prior revenue expectations, which it reaffirmed but did not restate in dollars in the release.

Third, fourth-quarter capital expenditures of four hundred fifty million to five hundred million dollars, and whether the lower second-half range holds.

Fourth, cost progress from seven thousand dollars per kilowatt on Phase One toward five thousand five hundred dollars on Cape Google Four Hundred, and, much later, the three-thousand-dollar long-term goal.

Fifth, execution on the Google plant: mid-twenty twenty-eight first power, a two point two billion dollar investment through twenty twenty-eight, and whether the six hundred megawatt option ever becomes a signed expansion.

Sixth, reservoir performance, including the Project Red temperature observation, and whether the doubled eight point four gigawatt Cape resource estimate begins to show up in additional contracted offtake, not only in a study.

Seventh, cash use against one point nine billion dollars of unrestricted cash and three hundred one point six million dollars of debt, as hiring, public-company costs, and construction all rise. General and administrative expense already jumped to thirty-nine point four million dollars from twenty-seven point four million dollars in the second quarter, and headcount rose by forty-five people, mostly in operations and construction. That is what a newly public builder looks like when it is staffing a multi-gigawatt pipeline. It is also a cost line that can keep growing even if the next GeoBlocks come in on schedule. The twenty million dollars of potential Department of Energy awards for appraisal drilling in Idaho and Nevada, and the additional twenty thousand acres of land, are modest next to Cape Station, but they are how a fifty-four point seven gigawatt early-stage pipeline starts to become a second geography, not only a single-site story in Utah.

If Phase One reaches one hundred megawatts on January first, investors will have a full winter of operating data before Google's mid-twenty twenty-eight first power. That operating data, plus the fourth-quarter spend, will say more than this quarter's one-day revenue figure ever could.

Let me close with a short recap.

Fervo reached first commercial operation at Cape Station on September thirtieth, but third-quarter revenue was only one hundred sixteen thousand dollars, a slight miss versus some estimates, with a seven-cent net loss to common stockholders that was either in line or a modest beat, depending on the source. The operating loss was still forty-three point seven million dollars, and reported net income was helped by interest income, a swap gain, and a tax-credit benefit. The company cut its second-half capital-expenditure range to seven hundred million to seven hundred fifty million dollars, reaffirmed prior fourth-quarter and twenty twenty-seven revenue expectations, and signed a three hundred ninety-six megawatt, fifteen-year take-or-pay agreement with Google that lifted binding contracted capacity to one thousand fifty-four megawatts and contracted revenue to about eleven point nine billion dollars. GeoBlocks Two and Three are aimed at commercial operation by January first, twenty twenty-seven. The follow-through is whether first power turns into a repeatable, lower-cost build, on schedule, for the much larger Google project, and whether the next two GeoBlocks meet the January first commercial-operation date that would complete Phase One. If they do, Fervo can start to be judged as an operator as well as a builder. If they slip, the eleven point nine billion dollar backlog will look further away than it does today.

That is the test from here. Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/09/fervo-energy-frvo-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/

Author: Fervo Energy

The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Fervo released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call the same day. On the call were Paxton Bentzinger, senior director of corporate development and investor relations; Timothy Latimer, co-founder and chief executive officer; and David Ulrey, chief financial officer. This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates. I will cover the results against expectations, the updated spending outlook, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next. Here is the headline. This was Fervo's first quarter with commercial operations, and the financials still look like a construction company more than like a power producer. The company declared commercial operation at Cape Station Phase One, GeoBlock One, on September thirtieth, ahead of the contractual commercial operation date. The first GeoBlock is a thirty-three megawatt unit, and it contributed only a single day of commercial operation in the quarter. Revenue was one hundred sixteen thousand dollars. The earnings release also shows fifty-five thousand dollars of revenue in the year-ago quarter, and two hundred ninety thousand dollars for the first nine months of twenty twenty-six. That revenue line slightly missed some published estimates. Seeking Alpha said G.A.A.P. earnings of a seven-cent loss beat by two cents, while revenue of twelve one-hundredths of a million dollars missed by three one-hundredths of a million dollars, which implies a consensus near one hundred fifty thousand dollars. TipRanks, citing The Fly, said the seven-cent loss was in line with a seven-cent consensus. I am not going to force those two earnings comparisons into a single official number. What is fair to say is that revenue was still tiny, as one day of commercial operation would suggest, and that the per-share result was either in line or a modest beat, depending on the estimate source, at a seven-cent net loss attributable to common stockholders. The net income line can confuse if you stop at the first figure. Fervo reported net income of eleven point seven million dollars, but a net loss attributable to common stockholders of twenty point eight million dollars, or seven cents a share. The Motley Fool takeaway noted that the per-share loss included fourteen million dollars of non-cash stock-based compensation. Net income reflected fifteen point four million dollars of interest income and two items the company called non-recurring: an eleven point eight million dollar non-cash gain on interest-rate swaps, and a twenty-nine point nine million dollar tax benefit from tax credits earned as Cape Phase One assets were placed in service. Operating loss was forty-three point seven million dollars. General and administrative expense was thirty-nine point four million dollars, up from twenty-seven point four million dollars in the second quarter, reflecting higher stock-based compensation, public-company costs, and headcount growth. Employees numbered three hundred six at quarter-end, up from two hundred sixty-one in the second quarter, primarily in operations and construction. item.title: Welcome to Dan's Reading List
item.description:
Welcome to Dan's Reading List.

This is a personal podcast of spoken summaries and readings from articles on the list. Each episode is generated from a plain text script, then added to this feed automatically.

In Podcast Addict, open an episode to hear it read aloud. The show notes link back to the original article. New episodes appear whenever a script is added to the reading list.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://github.com/dtrundle31-create/reading-podcast

Author: Dan
